articles.title: LA homelessness fraud cases expose deeper problem than stolen millions, oversight hawk warns
articles.summary: Rep. Michael Cloud says Los Angeles homelessness fraud cases expose a funding system that rewards program managers while keeping people in dependency.
articles.body:
Federal charges in Los Angeles reveal misuse of taxpayer funds in homelessness programs, prompting concerns about lack of oversight and effectiveness.

Rep. Michael Cloud highlights a systemic issue where corrupt providers benefit more than the homeless individuals the programs are meant to help, calling for better management of taxpayer dollars.

The focus shifts towards ensuring lasting outcomes and preventing fraud in federally funded homelessness programs, with calls for reform to incentivize oversight and proper management of funds.

Federal charges alleging that millions of dollars were siphoned from Los Angeles homelessness programs are exposing what one lawmaker told Fox News Digital is a deeper failure in the way Washington funds and measures such programs.

The latest cases out of Los Angeles fuel the concern of Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, that not only are corrupt providers stealing taxpayer money, but that the programs aren't meeting their goal of getting people off the streets.

"The only people really getting upward mobility in these programs, it would seem, is the people running the programs," Cloud told Fox News Digital after a House Oversight hearing examining federally funded homelessness programs in Los Angeles, Seattle and elsewhere.

"And that's not really what the program's supposed to be about."

Federal prosecutors charged three defendants Wednesday in separate homelessness fraud cases involving alleged misuse of taxpayer funds, including money allegedly spent on a nightclub and adjacent bingo hall and bribes allegedly tied to fake housing referrals.

Los Angeles' homelessness agency paid one of the suspect nonprofits more than $75 million, according to federal prosecutors, leading Cloud to seek out the real culprits blazing the money trail.

Cloud said the fraud itself is only one piece of a broader problem and that the system appears to reward spending and program activity without adequately measuring lasting outcomes.

Government too often judges success by "how much money we send out the door" instead of whether the spending is "actually helping people" or whether safeguards are in place to ensure taxpayer dollars are being used properly, Cloud said, describing the system as having been "incentivized for fraud."

"We've got to take those incentives out and get back to making sure that all these programs have incentives for oversight and that the dollars are managed well."

Some programs can keep a person "kind of in a cycle of dependency so that the program manager has job security, in a sense, and gets to live off the government dime," Cloud said.

"You [are seeing], as we begin to look into waste, fraud and abuse , why is it that these Democrat-led states are saying, 'No, we don't want the controls in place,'" he said, pointing to Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass' decision to step down from the LAHSA commission.

Los Angeles is not alone, he said, citing what has been called the feds' " Housing First " philosophy, generally prioritizing placing homeless in housing with less immediate regard for sobriety, mental health treatment or overall stabilizing services.

Cloud did not use the term "housing first" during the interview, but he described the concern behind that critique, arguing that some homelessness programs define success in ways that leave people dependent on government rather than moving toward independence.

Housing First is distinct from HUD's "Continuum of Care" framework, which is the local funding and coordination structure through which nonprofit providers, state and local governments and other organizations receive federal homelessness money.

In Los Angeles, LAHSA leads the local Continuum of Care, which HUD says received nearly $1 billion in taxpayer dollars over the previous five years.

Under Secretary Scott Turner, HUD moved to suspend LAHSA this year, citing alleged failures involving financial management, internal controls and safeguards against conflicts of interest. LAHSA has challenged the federal action in court.

"The 'housing first' experiment failed Americans by warehousing the vulnerable without results," Turner said in June when HUD announced a $4.04 billion Continuum of Care funding opportunity.

"This ideology promised to end homelessness. Instead, billions of taxpayer dollars were spent while homelessness increased to record levels."

That funding will focus on organizations aiding treatment and recovery, while setting aside $1.3 billion for new projects prioritizing transitional housing and supportive services and adding measures intended to prevent fraud, waste and abuse.

articles.title: Home guard slaps and drags woman by hair, arrested in Hyderabad
articles.summary: Home guard Kadiga Anand arrested and terminated for assaulting a woman near Hafeezpet railway station; Cyberabad police registered a suo motu case after video went viral.
articles.body: HYDERABAD: A home guard attached to the railway police was terminated from service by Cyberabad police commissioner M Ramesh on Saturday after he was found assaulting a woman near Hafeezpet railway station.Police also booked him in a criminal case and subsequently arrested him.The incident came to light after a video showing 36-year-old Kadiga Anand attacking the woman was circulated on social media.Director general of police CV Anand took note of the video and directed the Cyberabad police authorities to take action against the home guard.In the video, Kadiga Anand, who was in uniform, is seen repeatedly slapping the woman, grabbing her by the hair and dragging her before assaulting her in public.“On Friday evening, an incident was reported at Hafeezpet railway station wherein a Home Guard allegedly misbehaved with a woman, caught hold of her hair and dragged her. articles.title: Criança de 1 ano e 7 meses morre após ser atropelada na frente de casa | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente foi registrado em Birigui (SP), neste sábado (19). Segundo a polícia, motorista do casso fugiu sem prestar socorro e ainda não foi localizado. Morte da criança foi confirmada no local.
articles.summary: Uma criança de 1 ano e 7 meses morreu após ser atropelada por um motorista que fugiu sem prestar socorro na tarde deste sábado (19), em Birigui (SP).
articles.body:
Uma criança de 1 ano e 7 meses morreu após ser atropelada por um motorista que fugiu sem prestar socorro na tarde deste sábado (19), em Birigui (SP). Imagens de câmera de segurança registraram o momento. Veja no vídeo acima.

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, o pai do menino estava em casa, no bairro Jardim São Genaro, quando um carro parou em frente à residência. No banco do passageiro estava um amigo dele.

O pai foi chamado até a calçada para conversar com o conhecido e, conforme o relato dele à polícia, não percebeu que a criança também havia saído da casa.

Quando retornou para o interior do imóvel após finalizar a conversa, o homem escutou um estalo e, ao olhar para trás, viu que o filho havia sido atropelado. O pai tentou chamar o motorista do carro, que fugiu sem prestar socorro. Ainda de acordo com o registro policial, ele não tinha amizade com o condutor.

Criança de 1 ano é atropelada e motorista foge sem prestar socorro em Birigui (SP) — Foto: Portal Nossa Guia

O óbito de Guilherme Correa Lima foi confirmado no local. Equipes da Perícia Técnica e das polícias Civil e Militar atenderam a ocorrência. O caso foi registrado como homicídio culposo na direção do veículo automotor e fuga do local de acidente.

O suspeito foi identificado, mas, até a última atualização desta reportagem, não havia sido localizado.

O velório de Guilherme será realizado neste domingo no Memorial São Judas Tadeu, em Birigui (SP). O sepultamento será no Cemitério Municipal da Consolação.

articles.title: Condenado por estupro de vulnerável é preso trabalhando em açougue | G1
articles.standfirst: Homem foi preso no hipermercado onde trabalhava em Guarujá. Ele tinha sido condenado a 12 anos de prisão em regime fechado.
articles.summary: Homem foi preso no hipermercado onde trabalhava em Guarujá. Ele tinha sido condenado a 12 anos de prisão em regime fechado.
articles.body:
Açougueiro era procurado da Justiça e foi preso em Guarujá — Foto: Reprodução/Romu Guarujá

Um procurado da Justiça, condenado por estupro de vulnerável, foi preso em Guarujá , no litoral de São Paulo. De acordo com a Guarda Civil Municipal (GCM), ele foi encontrado no hipermercado onde trabalhava como açougueiro.

Uma equipe das Rondas Ostensivas Municipais (Romu) estava em patrulhamento na região do bairro Enseada na sexta-feira (18), quando foi informada do mandado de prisão em aberto contra o homem. Com base na denúncia, os agentes foram até o hipermercado, abordaram o açougueiro e confirmaram a ordem judicial contra ele por meio de consulta ao sistema.

Segundo a GCM, o suspeito havia sido condenado a 12 anos de prisão em regime fechado por estupro de vulnerável. Desta forma, o homem foi levado à Unidade de Pronto Atendimento (UPA) Rodoviária para avaliação médica.

Em seguida, ele foi encaminhado até a Delegacia Sede de Guarujá, onde o caso foi registrado como captura de procurado.

articles.title: Orion bate recorde de 19 anos e conquista Fita Azul da Refeno | G1
articles.standfirst: Trimarã pernambucano completou as 300 milhas náuticas até Noronha em 14h18min56s.
articles.summary: Trimarã pernambucano completou as 300 milhas náuticas até Noronha em 14h18min56s.
articles.body:
O barco pernambucano Orion Racing Brasil foi o primeiro à ilha na disputa da 37ª Regata Recife– Fernando de Noronha (Refeno), neste domingo (20). A embarcação conquistou o troféu Fita Azul e bateu o recorde da prova ao completar as 300 milhas náuticas, cerca de 545 quilômetros, em 14h18min56s ( veja vídeo acima ).

A conquista derruba uma marca que permanecia havia 19 anos. Desde 2007, o recorde da Refeno pertencia ao Adrenalina Pura, que havia completado a travessia em 14h34min54s. O barco também é o maior vencedor da competição, com dez troféus Fita Azul.

Orion conquista Fita Azul da Refeno — Foto: Cabanga/Divulgação

O Orion é um trimarã oceânico construído em fibra de carbono. A embarcação veio dos Estados Unidos e participou da regata pela primeira vez.

O barco tem como comandante Sérgio Avellar. Também fazem parte da tripulação Cláudio Teixeira, Guilherme Siqueira Araújo, João Pedro Monteiro Cardoso, Júlio Avellar, Marcus Duarte e Tiago Monteiro.

Um dos responsáveis por trazer o barco para Pernambuco, Cláudio Cardoso, contou que a embarcação participou da competição em defesa das pessoas com transtorno do espectro autista.

Dos 94 veleiros inscritos, 93 largaram no sábado (19), no Marco Zero da capital pernambucana. A única embarcação que não participou da travessia foi o Shiva IV. Segundo os organizadores, a comandante passou mal e decidiu permanecer na capital pernambucana.

A programação para receber os velejadores terá um evento, na segunda (21), na Praça do Porto de Santo Antônio, a partir da 17h. Entre as atrações estão DJ Flávia Pessoa; Mulheres que Bailam e Maracatu Nação Noronha – Ponto de Cultura e Memória Dona Nanete; Nego Noronha; Digão, da banda Raimundos; e Sony Bass.

A premiação da 37ª Refeno será realizada em 23 de setembro, no Museu do Tubarões.

articles.title: A forma correta de recuperar o sono perdido | G1
articles.standfirst: Apenas duas horas de sono a mais no dia seguinte podem ajudar a reverter os danos causados por uma noite mal dormida. Mas é preciso ter cautela na hora de dormir mais cedo ou acordar mais tarde.
articles.summary: Apenas duas horas de sono a mais no dia seguinte podem ajudar a reverter os danos causados por uma noite mal dormida. Mas é preciso ter cautela na hora de dormir mais cedo ou acordar mais tarde.
articles.body:
A forma correta de recuperar o sono perdido — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

Todos nós já passamos por isso: acordar de manhã com os olhos inchados, após uma noite mal dormida, nos sentindo exaustos.

"Tudo bem", dizemos para nós mesmos. "Vou recuperar o sono no fim de semana."

Para alguns, esta experiência ocorre apenas raramente. Mas, para outros, é uma forma de vida.

Uma pesquisa envolvendo cerca de 8 mil adultos americanos concluiu que cerca da metade dorme a mais regularmente nos fins de semana. E talvez não surpreenda saber que os adolescentes aparentemente formam o grupo que dorme até mais tarde no sábado e domingo, entre todas as faixas etárias.

Dormir um pouco a mais pode ser especialmente tentador para quem não consegue manter sono suficiente ao longo da semana.

A recomendação comum aos adultos é tentar dormir por cerca de sete a nove horas por dia, mas acredita-se que a maioria dos adolescentes precise de oito a 10 horas. E nem sempre é possível atingir estes números.

O que nos leva à pergunta que vale um milhão de dólares. Se não tivermos sono suficiente durante a semana, devemos dormir mais no sábado e no domingo? E, se dormirmos, poderemos compensar os efeitos do sono curto ao longo da semana?

Para podermos compreender as possíveis desvantagens de dormir até mais tarde, pode ser útil observar os dois principais processos que regulam o nosso sono.

O primeiro é a homeostase do sono, uma espécie de "reservatório de sono".

Quanto mais tempo ficarmos acordados, maior a nossa pressão para dormir. Com isso, também aumenta a sensação de que precisamos nos deitar e tirar uma soneca.

O segundo processo é o nosso ritmo circadiano, que é ajustado todos os dias pela exposição à luz e ao escuro, mudanças de temperatura e até pelos horários em que comemos ou nos movimentamos.

Estes dois processos trabalham em conjunto para nos sentirmos com sono todas as noites, idealmente em um horário apropriado.

Dormir por mais tempo para colocar o sono em dia pode desligar a homeostase do sono e o relógio circadiano. Isso ocorre quer você vá para a cama mais cedo ou durma até mais tarde.

Dormir por mais horas de manhã reduz a nossa pressão para adormecer ao longo do dia. Por isso, poderemos nos sentir cansados mais tarde naquela noite.

E, como não estamos apenas dormindo em um horário diferente, mas fazendo tudo o mais em outros horários (incluindo a nossa exposição à luz), o nosso ritmo circadiano também pode sair prejudicado.

O resultado? Poderemos dormir na manhã de domingo e adormecer mais tarde à noite.

Com isso, quando o despertador tocar às seis horas da manhã de segunda-feira, não teremos dormido o suficiente, recomeçando o mesmo ciclo.

"É como mudar de fuso horário toda semana", explica a psicóloga do sono Melynda Casement, diretora do Laboratório do Sono da Universidade de Oregon, nos Estados Unidos.

Deixar para recuperar o sono no fim de semana requer cuidado, mas, às vezes, pode ser uma boa ideia. Como esta prática pode nos deixar um pouco mais descansados?

As consequências da falta de sono à nossa saúde e cognição ainda estão em estudos.

Mas experimentos de restrição do sono cuidadosamente controlados deixaram claro que uma noite particularmente ruim prejudica a nossa fisiologia. E a recuperação do sono pode reduzir, e até reverter, pelo menos alguns desses prejuízos.

Em um estudo, por exemplo, pessoas que dormiram apenas duas horas em uma única noite apresentaram maiores níveis de dois tipos de leucócitos, o que pode indicar uma reação fisiológica ao estresse.

Alguns participantes puderam dormir por oito horas na noite seguinte. Ainda assim, seus níveis de glóbulos brancos não retornaram totalmente ao normal.

Mas os participantes que dormiram por até 10 horas no segundo dia apresentaram níveis de leucócitos quase idênticos aos verificados antes do estudo.

Outro experimento estudou o que acontece quando 11 homens que dormiam normalmente oito horas por noite tiveram seu sono limitado a quatro horas.

Seis noites de sono mais curto foram suficientes para prejudicar o metabolismo da glicose e a reação da insulina.

Se este regime de sono for mantido a longo prazo, as mudanças fisiológicas podem aumentar o risco de diabetes tipo 2. Mas, depois de mais seis noites dormindo por 12 horas, as avaliações dos participantes retornaram aos padrões iniciais.

Outros experimentos concluíram que recuperar o sono após uma noite sem dormir pode restaurar o nosso desempenho cognitivo.

Nada disso significa que dormir até tarde (ou ir para a cama mais cedo) no fim de semana combate todos os efeitos da falta de sono, especialmente quando os períodos de sono curto persistirem por semanas ou meses.

A atenção sustentada (nossa capacidade de permanecermos concentrados e reagir rapidamente) e nossa organização espacial parecem ser particularmente vulneráveis. E, nestes casos, mesmo a recuperação do sono no fim de semana não consegue reverter totalmente os efeitos da falta de sono de segunda a sexta-feira.

E existem também as sonecas. Elas podem ser benéficas para as pessoas que dormem pouco, mas são normalmente estudadas separadamente da recuperação do sono noturno.

Estes estudos foram realizados em condições artificiais de laboratório. O que acontece quando as pessoas recuperam o sono no mundo real?

Em um estudo na Suécia, pesquisadores acompanharam mais de 40 mil adultos por 13 anos. Eles concluíram que pessoas adultas com menos de 65 anos que dormiam regularmente por seis a sete horas por noite apresentaram menor risco de morte.

Por outro lado, os participantes que dormiam cinco horas ou menos tiveram risco de mortalidade 65% maior.

Entre os adultos com mais de 65 anos, não houve associação entre a falta de sono e o risco de mortalidade. Isso ocorre porque as nossas necessidades de sono diminuem à medida que envelhecemos, segundo indicam os pesquisadores.

Mas há um detalhe importante. Um fim de semana de sono decente aparentemente eliminou o aumento do risco entre as pessoas que dormem cinco horas ou menos. As pessoas que dormiam menos, mas recuperavam o sono no fim de semana, não apresentaram risco estatístico de morte maior do que as pessoas que dormiam por um período saudável ao longo da semana.

Mesmo quando a recuperação do sono perdido não reverte os efeitos de dormir pouco sobre a saúde, eles são frequentemente atenuados.

Em um estudo entre quase 2,8 mil participantes coreanos, por exemplo, as pessoas que, habitualmente, dormiam pouco apresentaram probabilidade cerca de 73% maior de sofrer de pressão alta. Mas cada hora de sono recuperado no fim de semana foi relacionada a cerca de 17% de redução do risco.

Outros estudos concluíram que as pessoas que dormem pouco durante a semana, recuperando o sono no sábado e no domingo, apresentam menor risco de demência.

Elas também têm menor risco de sofrer de síndrome metabólica, um conjunto de sintomas que eleva o risco de diabetes tipo 2 ou doenças cardiovasculares.

Mas nem todos os estudos encontraram benefícios entre pessoas que recuperam a falta de sono no fim de semana.

Um grande estudo realizado no Reino Unido não encontrou relação entre recuperar o sono e a mortalidade ou doenças cardiovasculares. Mas também não encontrou aumento dos riscos.

Consideradas em conjunto, estas conclusões ajudam a explicar por que alguns cientistas defendem que acordar no mesmo horário todos os dias, aconteça o que acontecer, pode ser contraproducente.

"Algumas pessoas chegam a dizer: 'Programe o seu despertador, mesmo nos fins de semana, para manter a sua regularidade'", afirma o professor emérito de cronobiologia Till Roenneberg, do Instituto de Psicologia Médica do Instituto LMU de Munique, na Alemanha. Mas ele discorda.

"É claro que você precisa recuperar o sono", afirma o professor. "O sono é uma das funções mais importantes da nossa vida."

A exceção são as pessoas que sofrem de insônia. O tratamento habitual desta condição recomenda que as pessoas evitem ir para a cama mais cedo e dormir até tarde.

Esta recomendação é válida mesmo após uma noite difícil, para evitar desregular o ritmo e dificultar ainda mais o sono.

A questão seguinte é o quanto você deve recuperar o sono para maximizar os benefícios, minimizando as desvantagens.

Existem cada vez mais evidências de que, para a maioria de nós, parece haver um "ponto ideal" de cerca de uma a duas horas de sono a mais.

Estudos nos Estados Unidos e na Coreia associaram este período à queda do risco de depressão e à redução das inflamações em adultos que costumam dormir pouco.

Os pesquisadores encontraram padrões similares entre pessoas mais jovens, incluindo menor risco de ansiedade e depressão.

Por isso, ficar na cama até um pouco mais tarde, às vezes, pode ser uma boa ideia. Mas, provavelmente, não irá justificar que você acorde na hora do almoço.

* Amanda Ruggeri é jornalista e estuda a ciência e a história das ideias que normalmente não questionamos. Ela escreve (em inglês) o curso online sobre Como Dormir Melhor, dividido em seis partes. Seu próximo livro, The Sleep Mith ("O Mito do Sono"), será lançado em meados de 2027.

articles.standfirst: Atendimento ocorre de terça (22) a quinta-feira (24) com bancos, concessionárias e lojas; senhas são entregues das 9h às 14h.
articles.summary: Saiba como participar; atendimento ocorre de terça (22) a quinta-feira (24) com bancos, concessionárias e lojas; senhas são entregues das 9h às 14h.
articles.body:
Mutirão de negociação de dívidas atende Sul do Rio e Costa Verde; Veja como participar — Foto: Divulgação/Procon-RJ

O Mutirão Estadual de Negociação de Dívidas irá atender os moradores do Sul do Rio e Costa Verde entre a terça (22) e a quinta-feira (24). A iniciativa, organizada pelo Governo do Estado, alcança 91 municípios fluminenses e reúne mais de 40 empresas e instituições para facilitar a quitação de débitos em atraso.

Segundo a Secretaria de Estado de Defesa do Consumidor (Sedcon) e o Procon-RJ, os consumidores podem renegociar pendências financeiras com bancos, operadoras de telefonia, concessionárias de serviços essenciais (água, luz e gás), além de redes varejistas e instituições de ensino.

A iniciativa vai acontecer em Angra dos Reis (RJ), Barra do Piraí (RJ), Barra Mansa (RJ), Comendador Levy Gasparian (RJ), Engenheiro Paulo de Frontin (RJ), Itatiaia (RJ), Mendes (RJ), Miguel Pereira (RJ), Paracambi (RJ), Paraíba do Sul (RJ), Paraty (RJ), Paty do Alferes (RJ), Pinheiral (RJ), Piraí (RJ), Porto Real (RJ), Quatis (RJ), Resende (RJ), Rio Claro (RJ), Rio das Flores (RJ), Sapucaia (RJ), Três Rios (RJ), Valença (RJ), Vassouras (RJ) e Volta Redonda (RJ).

Para ser atendido, o consumidor deve consultar a lista com os locais de atendimento presencial e as credenciadas no portal oficial do mutirão . A distribuição de senhas acontece das 9h às 14h. É necessário apresentar documento oficial de identificação com foto, CPF e comprovantes da dívida que pretende negociar.

articles.title: Acidente de ônibus em Cruzeiro: cinco morrem em queda de ribanceira | G1
articles.standfirst: Ônibus transportava cerca de 48 passageiros no trajeto entre Ipatinga (MG) e Aparecida (SP); cinco pessoas morreram após acidente e motorista ficou ferido. Um sexto morto foi confirmado após atendimento hospitalar.
articles.summary: O acidente de ônibus em Cruzeiro na Rodovia Doutor Avelino Júnior deixou cinco mortos em uma queda de ribanceira durante o trajeto de Ipatinga para Aparecida.
articles.body:
O ônibus que caiu em uma ribanceira de cerca de 15 metros na manhã deste domingo (20), em Cruzeiro (SP) , saiu da pista em um trecho de curva da Rodovia Doutor Avelino Júnior, próximo ao limite entre São Paulo e Minas Gerais.

Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, o ônibus transportava cerca de 48 passageiros e cinco pessoas morreram no acidente. As demais vítimas foram retiradas do veículo pelas equipes de resgate e encaminhadas para atendimento médico. Uma sexta morte foi confirmada após atendimento hospitalar.

O veículo fazia o trajeto entre Ipatinga (MG) e Aparecida (SP). Segundo apuração do repórter Gabriel Guimarães, da Rede Vanguarda , a placa do ônibus é de Lavras (MG) e não há identificação de empresa de transporte na lataria.

O motorista ficou ferido e foi levado para a Santa Casa de Lorena. A perícia está no local para investigar as circunstâncias do acidente.

Ônibus caiu em uma ribanceira de aproximadamente 15 metros na Rodovia Doutor Avelino Júnior, em Cruzeiro (SP). — Foto: Gabriel Guimarães/Rede Vanguarda

O Corpo de Bombeiros foi acionado por volta das 5h15. Equipes de Cruzeiro , Cachoeira Paulista, Lorena e Guaratinguetá atuaram no resgate, com apoio do Samu.

O ônibus caiu em uma ribanceira com aproximadamente 15 metros de desnível. Os feridos foram classificados inicialmente como vítimas leves e moderadas. A ocorrência permanece em andamento até a última atualização desta matéria.

articles.title: 'Party of comedians & jokers': PM Modi's mimicry at Rahul Gandhi's event draws BJP ire
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party on Sunday slammed Congress after a comedian mocked Prime Minister Narendra Modi while sharing the stage with leader .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party on Sunday slammed Congress after a comedian mocked Prime Minister Narendra Modi while sharing the stage with leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi at his "Chhatron Ki Goonj" event in Indore.In a social media post on X, Union minister Kiren Rijiju said the Congress has become "a party of comedians and jokers.""Congress Party has become a Party of Comedians & Jokers!" Rijiju said."They are out forever.... RIP," he added.Union education minister Pralhad Joshi also targeted Rahul Gandhi and accused him of stooping to an "absolute nadir of moral bankruptcy.""Rahul Gandhi and the Congress party have stooped to an absolute nadir of moral bankruptcy," Joshi said."Weaponising a student interaction to mock and insult the late mother of PM Modi ji reveals a shocking lack of basic human empathy and political culture," he added.BJP leader CR Kesavan also criticised Rahul, alleging that the Congress leader had shared the stage with individuals who mocked an elderly woman by referring to her as a "setting" and accused the Congress leader of laughing at the remarks."Rahul Gandhi shared the stage yesterday with cheap, vulgar trolls who insulted our Naari Shakti by mocking a frail elderly Mataji as a 'setting'," Kesavan said.Kesavan further alleged that the incident reflected an "uncouth culture" and claimed that such conduct was one of the reasons Rahul Gandhi had failed to connect with the youth.This comes after standup comedian Pulkit Mani shared the stage with Rahul and mimicked PM Modi during student-focused programme.During the 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' programme in Indore on Saturday, Rahul launched a sharp attack on the government over paper leaks and a host of student grievances.Rahul said the programme aimed to restore the "hope" that students had lost in the education system."We want the hope that was shattered in your hearts to return with renewed vigour. articles.title: In 2017, Dubuque turned recycled plastic equal to about 67,000 water bottles into 14 floating islands; the 2,674-sq-ft system now adds plant, fish and bird habitat to Bee Branch Creek
articles.summary: US News: Sometimes the answer for a city that has fought floodwaters for years isn’t more concrete, bigger pipes or taller walls. In Dubuque, Iowa, an old cree.
articles.body: Sometimes the answer for a city that has fought floodwaters for years isn’t more concrete, bigger pipes or taller walls. In Dubuque, Iowa, an old creek that was reopened became the site of an unusual experiment: 14 floating islands made partly from thousands of recycled plastic bottles. The islands were installed in 2017 as part of the Bee Branch Creek restoration and were designed to do more than just add greenery. Today, they help protect the creek, improve water quality and provide small pockets of habitat for fish, birds and aquatic life, states an online report by IECA News. Scroll down to read the details.Making a buried creek into an assetFlooding has been a problem in Dubuque for a long time, especially in the 7-square-mile Bee Branch Watershed, where more than half of the city's residents live or work. Repeated flash floods damaged some 1,300 homes and businesses, with widespread destruction to buildings, roads and stormwater infrastructure, adds the report.The city responded by daylighting the Bee Branch, a creek that had been buried in a storm sewer about a century ago. The waterway's reintroduction into the landscape allowed natural features to be incorporated into the flood mitigation project.A floating home built from recycled plasticThere are 14 islands totaling 2,674 square feet. Each island is a miniature replica of the natural archipelagos of the Mississippi River. Before the islands were placed in the creek, four prototype designs in a variety of shapes and sizes were developed, states IECA News. They constructed their primary floating structures from some 67,000 recycled BPA-free water bottles. Also, native plants were added along with carefully selected pieces of driftwood to create year-round useful habitat. And, fencing around the islands protects the new vegetation from waterfowl. Stainless-steel cables anchor the structures to the creek bed and the flexible anchoring permits the islands to shift with changing water levels and flow directions. The project was partially funded by grants and donations and cost $176,000, states the report.More than just floating gardensThe islands perform a variety of ecological functions. Their construction is such that their structures interrupt the wave energy and this helps to reduce erosion along the edges of the creek. They also serve as barriers to slow water as it moves around the islands, allowing suspended sediment to settle and helping keep the water clear. Now, plants absorb nutrients, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, on the islands. Preventing these nutrients from entering waterways can help reduce the amount of nutrients that eventually contribute to ecological problems downstream in the Mississippi River and Gulf of Mexico. Below the surface, the islands can be even more valuable. The plant roots and the floating structures provide space for biofilms, microorganisms that can help break down pollutants. The roots below the water also provide shelter to fish and juvenile aquatic species, and insects and crustaceans use the vegetation as part of the wider food web. And birds also use the islands as resting places and potential nesting habitat above the water.Keeping the islands in good healthAs per the report, the project also shows that nature-based infrastructure needs ongoing maintenance. The islands are regularly checked for buoyancy, vegetation and anchoring systems. A 2019 inspection found most plants were thriving, but some had to be replaced after animal interference and parts of protective fencing needed repairs. Dubuque’s experience shows that careful site selection, native vegetation, durable materials, secure anchoring and regular maintenance are important factors for other communities considering similar projects. What started out as a piece of a flood-control project has turned into something bigger: a working part of urban ecology. On Bee Branch Creek, recycled plastic is now the foundation of living habitat, and the floating islands show how flood infrastructure can create room for nature, as well.Images Courtesy: IECA News and istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: I loved capybaras before they were viral - I'm so glad they're having a moment
articles.summary: Filmmaker Sharon Walia explores the craze for capybaras in her latest documentary.
articles.body:
They look like giant guinea pigs, they eat their own poop, and the Vatican once declared that they were fish.

Capybaras - the world's largest living rodents - are unusual animals to say the least, and in recent years - helped by some high-profile capers - the capybara craze has gripped people across the world.

Now, a filmmaker has made a documentary all about them.

"I loved capybaras before they were viral, I've loved them for many, many years, but I'm so glad they're having a moment," says Sharon Walia, who explores the popularity of the huge herbivores in The Route to Cappyness.

"There's merch, there's kids with the school bags, there was the Oscar-winning film Flow which featured a capybara, and they're popping up everywhere on memes," Walia says.

"I don't even think this is a moment, I think this will last because it's been going on for years now and I just think people really, really love them."

The documentary is very different to Walia's first, which was, in her own words, "very distressing" to make.

"I was filming people literally drowning," Walia says of The Movement, which followed firefighter Brendan Woodhouse as he rescued refugees at sea.

She had the idea for the film while working as a journalist for Notts TV, a former local television channel in Nottingham, when she interviewed Woodhouse for a news story.

"He had resuscitated a baby off the Greek coast, it was a refugee family," she says.

"I said I would love to come and film when he was going back out on this mission.

"So I kind of just left my job and picked up a camera and I basically took a huge risk."

The risk paid off, as Walia managed to get her film distributed in cinemas and it was also picked up by Amazon.

By then, Walia knew she preferred making documentaries to filming news reports.

"I always felt with news it was too short," she says.

"I could never get the full story and go into depth like I wanted to. You end up having to cut it because your editor said it was too long. Longform was what I really wanted to do."

So she re-invested some of the money she made into her second film, The Keepers of the Pigs, billed as "the first ever documentary about guinea pigs".

"I wanted to do something very different to the refugee crisis," Walia says.

"I mean, I've always had guinea pigs and then I felt like no-one has ever really uncovered the history of the guinea pig.

"There was a local rescue in Wollaton [in Nottingham]. I went and filmed with them, and that ended up taking me to Peru to find out the history, because that's where they come from."

This film was picked up by Netflix, and again, shown in various cinemas and on Amazon Prime.

Her third documentary is therefore a natural follow-on.

"Capybaras are the world's largest rodent, and people call them 'guinea bigs' because they are like giant guinea pigs," Walia says.

"I love rodents. I think rodents get a bad rep generally, especially rats. I think people sometimes think rodents are dirty, smelly pests, and I would like to change that."

Capybaras are native to South America, and Walia's film begins in Brazil, where they roam free in the wild.

Walia met a man who has befriended 300 capybaras, before travelling to Florida and meeting a woman who shares her home with two of the giant rodents.

Walia also travelled to Japan, where capybaras are a symbol of peace and serenity.

She also filmed capybaras much closer to home, at Wheelgate Park in Nottinghamshire, and met a capybara which escaped from a zoo in Telford .

"It took me to four continents, filming this film, so it's been a bit of an adventure," she says.

The film will premiere at Broadway Cinema in Nottingham on Saturday, followed by further screenings across the UK.

It is also being released in the US, with the premiere being at AMC Cinema at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando.

"It's such a big achievement for the film, it kind of shows how much people do love the capybara," Walia says.

So why does she think they have become so popular?

"I think we're seeking something to connect us more, and capybaras symbolise kindness, co-existence, they get along with pretty much everyone, sometimes you see them hitching a ride with an alligator in the wild, they're so social," she says.

"So really with this film, I did set out to make a wildlife film and also focus on the viral aspect, but I ended up making a film about wellbeing, connection and slowing down."

articles.title: Yudh Abhyas 2026: M777 howitzers roar as Indian, US forces showcase firepower in Rajasthan
articles.summary: News News: Indian and US Army personnel conducted a live firing demonstration involving the M777 Ultra Light Howitzer at the Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajast.
articles.body: Indian and US Army personnel conducted a live firing demonstration involving the M777 Ultra Light Howitzer at the Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajasthan as part of Exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026, showcasing artillery capabilities and operational coordination between the two forces.According to the official update by the Indian Army, Indian gun crews demonstrated the M777's firing capabilities, while the visiting US contingent later interacted with Ultra Light Howitzer battery personnel at the gun positions to exchange operational knowledge and battlefield best practices.The live firing demonstration followed a lecture-cum-demonstration on the deployment of the M777 conducted at the Mahajan Field Firing Range on Wednesday. The session covered technical and tactical aspects of the artillery system, including the duties of key appointments, gun deployment, local defence coordination, movement to alternate positions during counter-bombardment and shoot-and-scoot drills, ANI reported.Exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026 is the 22nd edition of the India US joint military exercise, which began on September 15 and is being conducted over two weeks at the Auli Foreign Training Node in Uttarakhand and the Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajasthan. Around 600 personnel from each side are participating.According to the ministry of defence, the exercise is focused on enhancing the joint military capability of the two armies for the employment of Integrated Battle Groups in mountainous and semi mountainous terrain, with an emphasis on infantry dominated operations. It also aims to strengthen interoperability, facilitate the exchange of operational best practices and improve joint planning and execution.About the M777 howitzerThe M777 Ultra Light Howitzer is a 155mm, 39-calibre lightweight towed artillery gun developed for the US military. Its lightweight design allows it to be transported by military aircraft and helicopters, giving artillery units greater mobility and flexibility in difficult terrain.The Indian Army operates the M777 as part of its 155mm artillery fleet, with the system particularly relevant to India's requirements for high-altitude and mountainous areas because of its air-transportability and relatively low weight compared with heavier towed artillery systems.According to US Army, The M777 has a maximum range of about 24 km with unassisted ammunition, which increases to around 30 km with assisted projectiles. When equipped with compatible M982 Excalibur precision-guided ammunition, the M777A2 can engage targets at ranges of up to 40 km

articles.title: A Tennessee farmer spent 4 years trying to return a mistaken $20,000 IRS refund. Instead, he faced $4,000 in penalties; then country singer John Rich stepped in and ended the dispute
articles.summary: US News: After a four-year battle with the IRS, Wilson Perry Kirby, a Middle Tennessee farmer, finally got an acknowledgement that the government had indeed ma.
articles.body: After a four-year battle with the IRS, Wilson Perry Kirby, a Middle Tennessee farmer, finally got an acknowledgement that the government had indeed made a mistake. In 2022, Kirby received a $20,000 tax refund he knew wasn't meant for him. Instead of cashing it, he immediately tried to return the money. But instead, the IRS responded by charging him $4,000 in interest and withholding his own $1,800 refund, according to a report by WTVF. When the incident got media coverage, country music star John Rich saw the report and tried to untangle what four years of official channels couldn't fix. This month, Kirby finally received his refund, along with two apology letters from the agencies involved.The government’s mistake came at his expenseAll of Kirby’s trouble started in 2022, when the IRS sent him a $20,000 tax refund. Wilson Perry Kirby, a retired Montgomery County Highway Department worker and farmer from Coopertown, Tennessee, knew the money didn’t belong to him. So he contacted his accountant and filed the paperwork. They waited for the agency to acknowledge the error and process the return. That's where everything stalled.Instead of acknowledging the mistake and accepting the money back, the IRS charged him $4,000 in interest for holding on to it. Kirby was speechless: he hadn’t spent a penny, and in fact, all he did was try to return it. But the agency treated him like a debtor. To make it worse, the IRS withheld his own $1,800 tax refund to put towards the interest he supposedly owed.At this point, the Tennessee farmer was helpless. He reached out to anyone who might help, including government officials, his state senator's office, county representatives, the mayor, the governor and even the president's office. But none of his appeals were answered. A farmer trying to do the right thing got bureaucratic silence in return.This process dragged on for years and the stress mounted. He saw no resolution. It was absurd: a debt he didn’t owe was growing, while the IRS held back his $1,800 refund. The financial pressure and emotional toll broke him.Making things worse, Kirby lost his wife, Norma Jean, in August 2024. She was the one managing every aspect of his life, including the paperwork related to this trouble. Suddenly, he was all alone, both in life and in dealing with a problem he had been trying to resolve for years. He didn’t know how to navigate this federal nightmare alone. He was just an elderly farmer lost in grief, running the farm and fighting a battle against an agency that wouldn't acknowledge its own mistake. And for that, he was about to lose his own farm. An IRS notice reportedly warned Kirby that if he did not pay the interest it said he owed, he risked having his property seized.His battle made it to the newsWith no options left, Kirby turned to the media, hoping they could help him fight his battle. This spring, a reporter from WTVF brought the Tennessee farmer’s ordeal to light, detailing his four-year struggle with the IRS and the financial and emotional toll it had taken on him.The coverage caught the attention of John Rich, the country music artist appointed as Special Envoy for American Landowners. Rich, who was in Italy, saw the coverage and decided to step in, leveraging his position to untangle what four years of official channels couldn't. “Well, Mr. Kirby is a landowner, and his land is under threat, and he didn’t do anything wrong, and he is at his wits’ end with this thing, and I want to see what I can do,” Rich told the broadcaster.In a video shared on X in July this year, Rich assured viewers that Mr Kirby’s land wouldn’t be at risk and that the whole issue would soon be resolved. “Nobody is taking Mr Kirby’s farm. This is about to get HANDLED,” the singer said. Following this, in September, he met Kirby and assured him that the issue would be dealt with.Resolving the problem that was never his to begin withWhat Kirby has been waiting years to see has finally arrived. Earlier this month, he finally received his $1,800 refund that the IRS had withheld. The money surely mattered. But what mattered more was what came with it. John Rich drove out to Kirby's farm with two apology letters. Two formal acknowledgements from the agencies involved. They acknowledged the mistake. Kirby was right all along. “He says he almost took his own life over the thought of losing his farm, but we managed to save it,” Rich said in a post shared on X. “Big thanks to @SecRollins who fights like a Titan for our farmers every day, and is a true Patriot🇺🇸 ‘Love Thy Neighbor As Thyself’.”After four years, a grandfather and farmer finally got what he should have gotten in 2022: an acknowledgement of the truth. Kirby is relieved that the nightmare is finally over.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2007, an Australian geologist browsing Google Earth spotted an 850-foot circle in the outback; drilling later confirmed an iron-meteorite crater
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2007, Australian geologist Arthur Hickman identified a mysterious 850-foot circle in Western Australia's outback via Google Earth, leading to the discovery of Hickman Crater, one of Australia's youngest impact craters, confirmed through extensive drilling and analysis.
articles.body: In July 2007, a geologist scrolling through satellite images of Western Australia noticed a near-perfect circle in the outback. At the time, Arthur Hickman of the Geological Survey of Western Australia did not know he was looking at an impact crater, one that was later found to be among the youngest in Australia.A 260-metre crater in the PilbaraA study from the Australian Journal of Earth Sciences found that the size of the structure was around 260 metres (around 850 feet). The structure has been described by Australian Geographic as being the latest meteorite crater structure that has been discovered in Australia. This structure has been informally named the Hickman Crater.What the 2008 paper concludedThe first detailed published analysis came in the paper Hickman Crater, Ophthalmia Range, Western Australia: evidence supporting a meteorite impact origin, published in the Australian Journal of Earth Sciences. Authors Glikson, Hickman and Vickers reported a mean crater diameter of 260 metres. The lack of fragments from young volcanics younger than the Woongarra Rhyolite was not consistent with the explosive volcanic mechanism. Instead, the authors concluded that an impact had occurred, likely from a projectile about 10 metres wide that excavated a crater roughly 80 metres deep. It was dated to the Late Pleistocene period, with an age of between 10,000 and 100,000 years, due to the damming effect of the southern margin on a nearby creek.Why GSWA drilled in 2012Field evidence was not enough to raise a certainty. According to a 2017 news release from the Department of Mines, Industry Regulation and Safety (DMIRS), the Geological Survey of Western Australia ran the 2012 drilling project with Atlas Iron, which was already working in the area, to confirm early suspicions that the structure was a meteorite impact crater. Those results are laid out in the study Collaborative scientific drilling at Hickman Crater by P. W. Haines. The study describes a circular rim about 260 metres across that rises to 30 metres above a flat floor. The depth of the hole, drilled vertically in the aforementioned floor, was 64.7 metres. According to the 2012 drill core, the upper 48.4 metres is sediment that accumulated in the crater after it formed. At depths between 55.1 and 64.7 meters, there was very fractured rhyolite, which was the original bedrock.The crucial piece of evidence was chemistry. Ratios of platinum group elements in the breccia resembled those of meteorites much more than the ratios in the average continental crust, meaning a considerable meteoritic content. High nickel concentration indicated an iron meteorite. According to Haines, iron projectiles are the most common type to form small, simple craters like this one, even though chondrites are more common among meteorite falls overall, since stony projectiles of this size usually break up in the air.Why the impact left little shock damageHaines suggests that the projectile, estimated at about 10 metres across, may have been slowed significantly by the atmosphere before impact, which could have reduced shock pressures below the level needed to form the diagnostic planar deformation features while still leaving enough energy to excavate the crater. As has been suggested by Haines, the object may have been small enough to decelerate within the Earth's atmosphere before impact. As noted above, this appears to be the first scientific drill hole in a simple crater less than one kilometre in diameter in Australia, and possibly elsewhere.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2011, a British woman left London to circle the globe by bike, kayak and rowing boat; four years later, after a typhoon rescue and ocean crossings, she returned to London
articles.summary: UK News: Discover how Sarah Outen transformed her grief into an extraordinary 4.5-year global adventure, becoming the first woman to complete a solo row across the Indian Ocean and inspiring countless others along the way.
articles.body: Not every journey starts with a plan to alter the world. Some begin with a decision. One decision. To keep going after a loss. When Sarah Outen’s father died unexpectedly in 2006, the teenage rower turned her sadness into a solo crossing of the Indian Ocean, becoming the first woman to row the Indian Ocean solo and earning her a fellowship most people would spend a lifetime chasing.That was just the first chapter: Outen had made the first voyage, still an undergraduate at her Oxford college. Three years after graduation, in April 2011, she departed from Tower Bridge, London, on a journey she termed London2London: to traverse the entire northern hemisphere using only a bicycle, a kayak and a rowing boat.Starting from Tower BridgeIn theory, it was a simple plan. Outen would kayak over the Channel, cycle through Europe and Asia, row across the Pacific, cycle again through North America and ultimately row the Atlantic back to Britain. She thought she would get the full circle done in about two and a half years. In reality the earth had other plans, and the adventure would eventually take four and a half years and over 25,000 miles. Her history, on record at St Hugh's College, where she rowed for the college boat club before her first ocean journey, spans the complete arc from student rower to round-the-world explorer.Storms from the Pacific, rescue in the mid-oceanOuten’s first effort to row across the North Pacific in 2012 almost spelt doom for the entire mission. Less than a month into the voyage, her boat, the Gulliver, had been caught up in Typhoon Mawar, which meant she had to abandon the vessel and wait for the Japanese coastguard to take her out of the water. She spent months healing, both physically and emotionally, and then decided to return to Japan to give it another go.In 2013 she went off again in a new boat called Happy Socks and made it, becoming the first woman to row from Japan to Alaska. She even proposed to her partner on her satellite phone at one point during the voyage, bringing a moment of delight to a segment of the journey that had already pushed her to her limits. She paddled over a thousand miles north from Alaska with a paddling companion before switching to a bicycle called Hercules for a journey of North America during one of the worst winters the continent has seen in decades, with temperatures down to approximately minus 40 degrees Celsius.A narrow shave in the Atlantic, London boundThe last ocean section was just as pitiless as the first. Outen had spent 143 days at sea crossing the Atlantic east in 2015 before having to quit the passage and be evacuated due to Hurricane Joaquin, a choice she called one of the hardest of the whole expedition. Instead of giving up with the finish line in sight, she returned to complete the last stage, cycling and kayaking from Falmouth back to London.On 3 November 2015 Outen completed the loop by kayaking under Tower Bridge while friends, family and fans lined the banks of the Thames. By then she had already become the youngest person to do two solo ocean rows, one of several records to emerge from an expedition that had taken four and a half years rather than the two and a half originally intended.Later, Outen wrote about the experience in her book Dare to Do. 'The trek was as much an emotional test of resilience as a physical one,' she said. Her narrative today inspires young people to achieve big ambitions, a fitting legacy for an adventure that began with a commitment to make something of grief and concluded with a roaring audience welcoming her home to London.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Delhi pollution crackdown: Hotspots to be mapped, pending road works get Oct 31 deadline
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Delhi government has stepped up its crackdown on air pollution, directing district administrations to map pollution hotspots, identify .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Delhi government has stepped up its crackdown on air pollution, directing district administrations to map pollution hotspots, identify sources within a three-kilometre radius and assign agencies specific corrective measures and deadlines. The government has also set October 31 as the target for completing pending road and civil works, wherever feasible. It ordered tighter action against road dust, construction pollution, waste burning, illegal parking and traffic congestion.The directions were issued during district-level review meetings chaired by Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa for East, North-East, South-East and South Delhi. Officials were told to use AQI monitoring data to identify problem areas, assess the sources driving pollution and take immediate action at the ground level.Hotspots to get source-specific action plansDistrict administrations will map pollution hotspots based on data from AQI monitoring stations. Each hotspot will then be assessed for sources such as road dust, traffic congestion, vehicular emissions, construction and demolition activity, unauthorised parking, open or uncovered areas and biomass or waste burning.Where applicable, pollution-generating activities within a three-kilometre radius of each hotspot will also be examined.Authorities will prepare source-wise action plans setting out the remedial measure, the agency responsible and the timeline for implementation.Locations recording high levels of PM10 and PM2.5 will receive focused attention, particularly areas with heavy traffic, heavy-vehicle parking, significant road dust and congestion. Such locations will be inspected for their pollution sources and immediate remedial action will be taken.October 31 target for pending road worksThe government has directed agencies to complete pending civil works on priority and by October 31, wherever feasible.These include pothole repairs, treatment and development of brown areas and other road and roadside works. Officials have also been told to maintain completed works properly to reduce road-dust generation.Where essential works cannot be completed because other projects are still underway, agencies will have to continue water sprinkling and other dust-suppression measures until the road surface is restored.Construction, waste burning face tighter actionThe government has directed agencies to strictly enforce dust-control norms at construction and demolition sites. Violations will attract stringent action under applicable rules.The ban on biomass burning will also be enforced without exception. Preventive measures will be strengthened against the open burning of garbage, plastic and rubber waste, textile and fibre waste, industrial and organic residues, scrap and other combustible material.Illegal parking and encroachments targetedOfficials were also directed to remove illegal encroachments from roads and public spaces where they contribute to congestion and obstruct traffic movement.The move is aimed at improving traffic flow and reducing pollution caused by idling vehicles and prolonged traffic movement.At Anand Vihar Bus Terminal, agencies have been directed to step up enforcement against unauthorised parking of buses and heavy vehicles. articles.title: India's defence industry takes off: The numbers explained
articles.summary: News News: Over the past decade, India's domestic defence industry has steadily grown, and recently released numbers show the scope and size of this growth. Indi.
articles.body: Over the past decade, India's domestic defence industry has steadily grown, and recently released numbers show the scope and size of this growth. India, still one of the largest defence importers, has steadily, over this time frame, reduced dependence on imported weapons, platforms, systems and sub-systems across the three services, as well as for exports. This shift is being driven by a combination of higher defence spending, changes in procurement policy, growing private-sector participation, and greater investment in research and development.Big transformation in defence sector The scale of this transformation becomes clear when you look at production figures. Defence output touched a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26, up 15.6% from Rs 1.54 lakh crore the previous year, and more than double what it stood at just five years earlier in 2020-21, when the figure was Rs 84,643 crore. Compare that to Rs 43,746 crore back in 2013-14, and the trajectory of this growth becomes hard to miss. The Centre too has set an ambitious target of Rs 3 lakh crore in annual production and Rs 50,000 crore in exports by 2029.This growth has been underpinned by a defence budget that has more than tripled since 2013-14, rising from Rs 2.53 lakh crore to Rs 7.85 lakh crore in 2026-27. Capital expenditure, the portion that actually funds acquisition and development of new platforms, has climbed even more sharply and more than doubled from Rs 94,587.95 crore in 2014-15 to Rs 2.19 lakh crore in 2026-27. This subdivision of the overall defence budget matters because this is the money that directly finances military modernisation rather than routine running costs that are counted under the revenue head of the budget.Defence exports steal the spotlightBut if there's one number that best captures how far India has come, it's exports. From a modest Rs 686 crore in 2013-14, defence exports have grown more than 56 times, hitting a record Rs 38,424 crore in the last financial year. This was also a remarkable growth of 62.66% over the Rs 23,622 crore recorded the year before, with Indian-made defence products now reaching over 80 countries.What's particularly striking is the increased share of private companies, which accounted for Rs 17,353 crore, or 45.16%, of these exports, nearly matching the Rs 21,071 crore, or 54.84%, contributed by the nation's well-established defence public sector undertakings. This is still a considerable shift as the country's defence sector was once dominated almost entirely by these government-run entities.The pattern holds in overall production too, with defence Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) and public entities accounting for around 76% of total output, while the private sector's share has climbed to its highest level yet at 24%, contributing roughly Rs 42,000 crore during the year.Defence production a key strategic asset In the current global environment, military capability to sustain long wars is the major currency of power. This is evidenced in all global conflicts,Military capability is a matter of men and material in the correct mix. Nations which have invested in building this capability indigenously will not only be victorious but will also be great powers. Self reliance in defence is an insurance against defeat and is a guarantor of victory. In this context the time has for India to invest more in spending on defence to achieve great power status.In terms of war-fighting capability, this expanding industrial base means more than just impressive headline numbers. A larger domestic manufacturing capacity can potentially shorten the time needed to replenish ammunition, repair damaged equipment, and scale up production during a prolonged crisis, while also giving the armed forces greater control over upgrades and modifications without complete dependence on overseas suppliers. This has become a critical aspect as the extended conflicts in West Asia and Eastern Europe have shown the importance of a domestic defence industrial base and, in the age of sanctions, can help a nation stay in the fight without concerns of its weapon supplies being cut off.This push has reshaped procurement itself. The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) has cleared Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) for more than Rs 6 lakh crore worth of systems designed by DRDO and manufactured by Indian industry. Some of the largest such programmes involve combat aircraft and helicopters, including the second order for 97 Tejas Mk-1A fighters worth around Rs 62,000 crore and 156 LCH Prachand light combat helicopters valued at roughly Rs 62,700 crore, programmes designed not just to equip the forces but also to strengthen domestic defence manufacturing capability.These procurement reforms have evolved steadily over the years. The Defence Procurement Procedure of 2016 laid the groundwork for greater emphasis on domestic manufacturing, while the Defence Acquisition Procedure of 2020 strengthened indigenous procurement further and expanded opportunities for Indian companies across design, development and production. The Defence Procurement Manual 2025 has since sought to streamline nearly Rs 1 lakh crore worth of revenue procurement, while the still-under-consideration Defence Acquisition Procedure 2026 is looking to simplify the acquisition categories, provide support for indigenous design and improve indigenous content requirements.Private industry and innovation to pave the road aheadStartups and smaller innovators are deliberately being pulled into this ecosystem. The Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) scheme has engaged 676 startups, MSMEs and innovators, resulting in 551 design and development contracts by March 2026. This has been backed by an outlay of Rs 498.78 crore. The Acing Development of Innovative Technologies with iDEX (ADITI) scheme was separately approved with Rs 750 crore for 2023-24 through 2025-26 to support critical defence technology development, while the Technology Development Fund (TDF) offers grants of up to Rs 50 crore per project, with 80 projects worth Rs 334 crore under implementation as of June 2026, alongside an additional Rs 500 crore corpus sanctioned specifically for deep and emerging technologies.DRDO itself has significantly ramped up technology transfer to industry. Its Development cum Production Partner (DcPP) framework has now transferred technologies to 134 partner companies, with 2,180 technology transfer agreements signed and more than 2,780 intellectual property rights opened up for industry use by March 2026. The government's Positive Indigenisation Lists, ten of them so far, five each under the Department of Military Affairs and the Department of Defence Production, have identified 5,521 items the armed forces are now expected to source domestically. A marketplace such as the Srijan Defence Equipment Empowerment Platform has connected over 41,000 vendors and 2.7 lakh products into this sourcing ecosystem, effectively serving as a digital repository for indigenous defence procurement.Defence R&D allocation increased from Rs 13,716.14 crore in 2014-15 to Rs 29,100.25 crore in 2026-27, a jump of more than 112%, and since 2022-23, a full 25% of the defence R&D budget has been thrown open to industry, startups and academia. Government testing infrastructure has been opened up too, with facilities across 24 DRDO laboratories now accessible through the Defence Testing Portal, letting manufacturers and startups use specialised government facilities to validate their own systems.Indigenising inventories one step at a time The results of all this are already visible in what's actually being fielded. The Army has achieved around 91% self-sufficiency in ammunition, having indigenised 159 of the 175 variants in its inventory, a particularly critical achievement given how central ammunition stocks are to sustaining prolonged operations.These developments point to a defence sector that is now growing both vertically and horizontally, a sector built around design, research, testing, production, maintenance, upgrades and exports as a single connected ecosystem. These moves have implications for strategic autonomy, since a military overly reliant on imports remains vulnerable on spare parts, ammunition and technical support during a crisis, even as building domestic capacity doesn't eliminate imports altogether or guarantee every component can be produced economically at home.

articles.title: Colorado Mesa University buried 471 geothermal boreholes 500 feet underground; they now heat and cool 16 buildings while saving about $1.5 million a year
articles.summary: US News: Explore how Colorado Mesa University's geothermal heating and cooling system, featuring 471 boreholes, enhances energy efficiency while saving $1.5 million each year across 16 buildings.
articles.body: Hundreds of boreholes form the underground part of a geothermal heating and cooling network beneath Colorado Mesa University’s campus in Grand Junction, Colorado. The system currently connects 16 buildings and serves about 1.2 million square feet of space, and the U.S. Department of Energy says it saves the university about $1.5 million in energy costs each year.The installation began with a single borehole field beneath the campus, and it has since grown into a larger network connected by a central loop that runs across the university. The underground infrastructure uses the relatively stable temperature of the ground as part of the process of moving heat between buildings.The system started with one buildingColorado Mesa began planning its geothermal system in 2007, when the university was preparing Dominguez Hall. The building needed to meet energy-efficiency requirements to receive state capital construction funding. University officials and their design teams selected geothermal heat pumps instead of installing a conventional heating and cooling system. The first installation used a borehole field about 500 feet below campus and was connected to the single new building.According to the Department of Energy, the original borehole field eventually became part of four fields connected by an 18-inch central pipe running from the southern end of campus to the north, and the central loop now serves 1.2 million square feet across 16 buildings. The exact number of underground boreholes has also grown beyond the roughly 450 figure that is sometimes used in descriptions of the system. A National Renewable Energy Laboratory analysis documented 471 boreholes, with the fields reaching depths of up to 500 feet, and the same analysis reported that the system was serving 16 buildings spread across roughly 110 acres.Heat moves through the campusThe system uses geothermal heat pumps and a closed-loop network to transfer heat, and during cold weather, the ground provides a heat source for the buildings. During warmer periods, the system reverses the process and moves heat away from buildings, and that makes the same infrastructure useful for both heating and cooling. The Department of Energy says that the system provides about 90% of the heating and cooling that is required to operate the campus. When the central loop becomes too warm, excess heat can also be transferred to the university’s Olympic-sized swimming pool and irrigation system, which serve as heat sinks.Colorado Mesa University’s own current description lists 16 connected buildings, 2.5 miles of central loop pipe and 1.2 million square feet of academic and auxiliary space served by the geo-exchange system. It also reports annual energy-cost savings of about $1.5 million.The network is still expandingColorado Mesa has continued to add facilities and expand the underground infrastructure. In 2026, the university reported that its thermal energy network was being expanded beneath the rugby pitch, and hundreds of additional underground wells and miles of piping were planned to connect nearby residence halls and other buildings. The university said that the expansion would allow heat energy to move between buildings based on demand and could store heat underground when it was not immediately needed. The Department of Energy's case study puts total energy-cost savings at $15.9 million since 2008, while the university's current figures put annual savings at about $1.5 million.The underground network is a campus-wide heating and cooling system that has expanded from one borehole field and one building to hundreds of boreholes, a central loop and 16 connected buildings, with further expansion underway, and therefore functions as more than a single geothermal installation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1942, a 24-year-old WWII pilot vanished over Egypt; 84 years later, his family finally buries him beside his parents in North Carolina
articles.summary: US News: More than eight decades after his death during World War II, Captain Marvin Lancaster has been laid to rest in Vanceboro, North Carolina alongside his.
articles.body: More than eight decades after his death during World War II, Captain Marvin Lancaster has been laid to rest in Vanceboro, North Carolina alongside his parents. Family, friends and fellow service members gathered in Epworth Methodist Church to lay Lancaster to rest on Friday. “Right now, oddly enough, I’m feeling relief,” Lancaster’s nephew Jerry Brown said, as per a report by WITN. “The road has come to an end, and Marvin will be here. That’s where he belongs, with his brothers and his parents and his grandparents.”He arrived in a flag-draped casket, carried by airmen and Marines young enough to be his great-grandchildren, and when they laid him down, the younger brother Lancaster last knew as a 2-year-old boy hobbled over on a cane and dropped a carnation in a tribute. “Long time coming,” said his brother Ted, his beard gone white.In 1942, Lancaster was only 24 when his fighter plane, a P-40F Warhawk, went down over Egypt in the early months of World War II, attacked by German fighters midair. British forces recovered only the remains of an unidentified pilot, eventually burying them in Tunisia among other nameless fighters.Lancaster left a family of 15 brothers and sisters on a tenant farm back in tiny Vanceboro, home to only about 800 people then. Before, during and after the war, his paychecks pulled the family through rural poverty and gave him an almost mythical status among his younger brothers and sisters. Two of his nephews — Jack and Jerry Brown — grew up admiring the uncle they knew only from pictures, a ghost grinning at them in a flight suit. Jack Brown flew missions for the Marines over Vietnam; Jerry for the Navy during the Yom Kippur War of 1973, which brought him within 70 miles of his uncle’s crash site.Magic of DNAMore than 70,000 Americans remain missing from World War II, and for decades, Brown pressed for answers that wouldn’t come. He found his uncle’s name on the wall at the US cemetery in Tunisia, and because so few soldiers there remained unidentified, he figured he must be among them. He collected Lancaster’s after-action report and even spoke to German pilots who fought there on the same day. But by 2014, he had largely given up the hunt. One year later, the Defence POW/MIA Accounting Agency started up, merging a tangle of government offices that didn’t always work together well, and nine years later the Brown family got the long-awaited call about a DNA match.His remains went unidentified for more than 80 years, until his family received answers in December 2025.“That’s why he’s here,” Brown said Friday. “The magic of DNA and the persistence of a data analyst stuck in the bowels of an office who wanted to take a name off a wall.” “When the casket came off the aeroplane, and they invited us to touch it, it was such a powerful emotion,” Jerry Brown said.Jack Brown was inspired by his uncle's story to become a fighter pilot in the Marine Corps. “This is just such a special, emotional time to honour a good and courageous man and a nice American,” Jack Brown said.Jack Brown rose to speak and noted that their family might not have grown so large and successful if not for the Army checks that came home to Vanceboro until 1949, seven years after his father, Augustus, received his son’s belongings in a box. “A man’s worth at the end of his life cannot be summed up in an inventory of his personal effects,” Brown said. “We have only to look around us, and we’re seeing family we haven’t seen for years, second and third generations I’ve only heard about. Largely because of my uncle’s support after his death. ... What a fine and good man he was.”Lancaster's funeral fell on National POW MIA Recognition Day, which honours those who, like Lancaster for decades, have yet to make it home. Jerry Brown said his family is grateful to the Defence POW/MIA Accounting Agency for its work to identify his uncle.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ​Meet Apollin Lu, the 17-year-old British Columbia student who mobilised 140+ volunteers to rescue nearly 9,000 pounds of farm produce
articles.summary: US News: Apollin Lu is only 17, but she is already leading a growing youth network that is helping tackle food waste across British Columbia. She founded the F.
articles.body: Apollin Lu is only 17, but she is already leading a growing youth network that is helping tackle food waste across British Columbia. She founded the Food Recovery Alliance, which has mobilised more than 140 young volunteers who have saved 9,000 pounds of fresh produce from going to waste. Together, they collected surplus produce from local farms and redistributed it to shelters and community organisations. Lu was recognised with the 2026 Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes for her efforts to reduce food waste and help people in need.She saw food waste up closeApollin Lu grew up on her family’s garlic farm. She watched her father work the soil for a decade. Her neighbours also had farms, and she noticed a pattern. Lots of this fresh produce ended up going to waste. Farmers weren’t discarding vegetables out of negligence. They were managing supply chains that didn’t always align with demand. She started asking herself: why is good food going to waste while people in the community are starving? For the farmers, the wastage was part of the business, but for the underprivileged communities nearby, it was a lost meal.By the time she got into ninth grade, she knew she had to do something. So she formed the Food Recovery Alliance to address that discrepancy. The work began quietly. Lu spent two years doing exactly what most non-profit founders do at the start: cold-calling farmers, building trust with storefront managers and convincing her peers that weekend farm work sounded fun. Eventually, the farmers joined her programme. By now, her team had built an invoicing app so that farmers receive a tax receipt the moment food is donated. Along with her volunteers, she also put together a community garden where younger students grow fresh produce and donate it, while also learning sustainable farming. By the time the organisation was formally incorporated under the BC Societies Act in February 2025, it had already collected 7,272 pounds of produce valued at over $25,210. “This year we really started to get a lot of youth interest in our organisation, which I think will help us sustain long term,” Lu told Victoria News.Over the past three years, Lu has collected 9,000 pounds of locally grown crops, valued at more than $32,000, from farmers across Greater Victoria and Vancouver, and donated them rather than allowing them to end up as waste.From farms to familiesFood Recovery Alliance fills a crucial gap. Every year, farms yield more than they can market. Retailers and wholesalers pass on imperfect or surplus stock. So the organisation partners with Mustard Seed to collect and redistribute this excess produce to people in need. The organisation processes more than 10,000 pounds of rescued food each week from 30-plus donors, reaching roughly 70,000 food-insecure people across the region.Food Recovery Alliance slots directly into that gap. Volunteers show up at farms during harvest season and gather what would otherwise go unharvested or unsold. They coordinate delivery to non-profits, which then redistribute it. Though the scale is smaller than retail partnerships, the impact is direct and the relationships more human.“It’s hard for a lot of farmers to trust someone they don’t know to come on their farm. We really want to partner with Rise Up and other organisations, to spread the word and build legitimacy,” Lu told the outlet. After building legitimacy, the organisation is now piloting partnerships with organisations such as Rise Up, aiming to expand its credibility as it grows its Vancouver network.Recognition and awardApollin Lu is now a Grade 11 student at St. Michaels University School (SMUS) in Saanich. She grabbed national attention after winning the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes, which annually recognises 25 young leaders aged 8 to 18 whose service work demonstrates a public impact. She is among the 2026 winners and a top-tier recipient of a $10,000 award. For Lu, the recognition validates what she already knows from the work itself: that youth-led initiatives can scale.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
