articles.title: In 2001, a 24-year-old Englishman cycled out of Yorkshire to see the world; four years and 46,000 miles later, he came home after crossing 60 countries
articles.summary: UK News: Discover the inspiring story of Alastair Humphreys, who cycled 46,000 miles across five continents, exploring 60 countries in a quest to see the world.
articles.body: On a summer morning in 2001, Alastair Humphreys left his home in Yorkshire on a bicycle with a deceptively simple plan: keep riding until he had travelled around the world. He was 24 and had recently finished his studies, but instead of settling into a conventional career, he chose to spend the next several years on the road. What began as an ambitious idea became a 46,000-mile journey through 60 countries and five continents, lasting more than four years.According to Alastair Humphreys, he eventually returned to Britain in November 2005 after crossing deserts, mountains, savannahs, highlands and frozen landscapes. His route stretched from England through Europe, the Middle East and Africa, across the Atlantic to South America, northwards to Alaska, across the Pacific to eastern Siberia and then west through Asia and Europe.From Yorkshire to AfricaThe starting point for Humphreys' journey was Airton, near Skipton, in August 2001. It proved to be a task in itself to get accustomed to the magnitude of the endeavour. As he explained in his account of the expedition, "it turned out to be much tougher in practice than just imagining it on a map or discussing it with friends." Initially, he moved south, passing through parts of Europe and Africa. He passed through countries including Albania, Sudan, Ethiopia and Zimbabwe. Temperatures in Sudan reportedly reached 45°C, and parts of the African leg were especially remote and desolate.This expedition was mostly self-financed. Humphreys had around £7,000 in savings before starting his journey and also received some financial assistance through sponsorship. In his personal account, he says that this journey had to be highly dependent on his savings because, apart from receiving some help like equipment, nothing else came his way. He also took this opportunity to create awareness for his charity named Hope and Homes for Children.According to research published in the Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, prolonged ultra-endurance cycling can cause substantial physiological changes, including alterations in energy balance and recovery during extended periods of exertion. The findings provide a scientific perspective on the physical demands Humphreys would have faced during a journey that required cycling for thousands of miles across varied terrain and climates.Across Oceans and into extremesAfter cycling through Africa, Humphreys reached Cape Town and crossed the Atlantic by yacht. He then began one of the most demanding stretches of the expedition: cycling from Patagonia towards Alaska. According to the Guardian, his route through South America included long sections of difficult terrain before he continued north through the Americas. By August 2004, he had already crossed four continents and 44 countries, with Alaska still ahead. His reports described cycling from Peru through landscapes that ranged from desert to high mountain country before eventually reaching North America.Unlike a simple nonstop circuit of the globe, Humphreys' journey included several sea crossings because he could not cycle across the oceans. He had to undertake trips across the oceans by ship where it was not possible to cycle and other routes due to geographical factors. After landing in Alaska, Humphreys sailed via a freighter across the Pacific Ocean to the east coast of Siberia. Thereafter, the bicycle was used to travel around the rest of Russia and into Asia. The Siberia leg was again an extreme environment. Humphreys travelled from the extreme heat of Africa to the extreme cold of Russia.46,000 miles laterWhen Humphreys undertook his last ride in Europe, four years had already passed since he started riding his bike away from Yorkshire. Humphreys' bike had taken him to 60 different countries on five continents within 1,555 days of travel, which was recorded in Humphreys' expedition diary. In November 2005, Humphreys returned to Britain at age 28. According to The Guardian, Humphreys travelled for four years and covered 45,000 miles, while Humphreys said his final total was 46,000 miles.What started as a 24-year-old's decision to leave Yorkshire and see what was beyond his doorstep eventually became a four-year journey across much of the world. By the time Humphreys returned home, his bicycle had taken him through 60 countries and across landscapes that could hardly have been more different. The ride had ended, but the experience had turned a simple urge to explore into a remarkable story of life on the road.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: North Korea fires two ballistic missiles off east coast in three hours
articles.summary: SEOUL, Sept 20 () - North Korea launched two missiles off its eastern coast on Sunday, its second set of tests in roughly a week and days after Pyongyang acc...
articles.body:
SEOUL, Sept 20 (Reuters) - North Korea launched two missiles off its eastern coast on Sunday, its second set of tests in roughly a week and days after Pyongyang accused the ‌US of driving tensions on the Korean Peninsula through a series of military drills.

Just three hours ‌after launching a short-range ballistic missile (SRBM) toward the East Sea on Sunday afternoon, North Korea fired another short-range ballistic missile, according ​to South Korea's defence ministry.

If the subsequent launch is confirmed to be a ballistic missile, it will mark two consecutive ballistic missile tests by North Korea within a three-hour window.

South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the first test firing from the Wonsan area around 3 p.m. (0600 GMT), identifying the weapon as a ‌ballistic missile. Japan's defence ministry also said ⁠it appeared to be a ballistic missile.

Japanese public broadcaster NHK said the projectile had come down outside Japan's exclusive economic zone.

The first projectile flew approximately 450 km (280 miles) and ⁠is presumed to belong to the Hwasong-11 series, according to South Korea's military. The second short-range missile, which was also fired from Wonsan at about 5:50 p.m. (0850 GMT), flew more than 600 km (373 miles), it said.

"South Korean and ​US ​intelligence authorities have been tracking and sharing related developments ​from the initial stage of the launch, and ‌have also shared information regarding the 'North Korean ballistic missile' with Japan," the South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff said.

South Korea's National Security Council condemned the short-range missile launch, which follows a test on September 12. The council urged Pyongyang to immediately cease missile activity, warning the test directly violated UN Security Council resolutions.

Japan also lodged a protest through embassy channels in Beijing, according to a Nikkei report.

"This series of North ‌Korean actions threatens the peace and security of Japan, the ​region, and the international community," Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi ​was quoted as saying by Nikkei.

On Saturday, North ​Korea dismissed a resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog against Pyongyang's nuclear programme.

Pyongyang ‌last week also condemned a US-led naval drill ​which included South Korea and ​Japan and which ran from August 29 to September 10 near Guam.

North Korea's Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, on Friday blamed US-led military drills for "ever-worsening" tensions ​on the Korean Peninsula and ‌vowed no change in the country's course to strengthen its nuclear arsenal.

(Reporting by Cynthia Kim ​and Heejin Kim in Seoul and Junko Fujita in Tokyo, additional reporting by Sumedha Mukherjee ​in Bengaluru; Editing by William Mallard and Michael Perry)

articles.title: Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses moral high ground by living in tax exile - Labour Party Chair
articles.summary: The billionaire businessman told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.
articles.body:
The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Bridget Phillipson said she would take the billionaire businessman's comments that the UK was "on the slide" with a "pinch of salt".

Sir Jim, the founder of petrochemical giant Ineos and Manchester United's co-owner, told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020 and said "things would have to get better" in the UK for him to return.

When questioned over the remarks, Phillipson said Sir Jim loses "the moral high ground" by "making these kinds of pronouncements while choosing to make decisions, that he is within his rights to make, to become a tax exile".

Pushed on whether it bothers her that people who create jobs and pay a lot of tax were leaving the UK, the minister said she was "optimistic about our country's prospects".

Other high profile billionaires have left the UK, including including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently the UK's third biggest taxpayer, hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.

But, Philipson argued the country was in a good position ahead of the Budget next month, and Andy Burnham has shown a "sense of hope and optimism whilst recognising that many families are still struggling and there is more to do."

"Of course, there are challenges, including big international headwinds, but I fundamentally believe that we are in a strong position going into this budget because of the decisions taken over the last two years, and I believe our country's best days lie ahead of us," she said.

Philipson declined to speculate over whether there would be tax rises in the Budget on 28 October, and said the government remained committed to being disciplined about its spending rules.

Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be about £15bn, also criticised the government for failing to invest further in North Sea oil and gas, claiming it amounted to "insanity".

"You would expect [the government] to exploit our natural resources and we're clearly not doing that. We're shutting it down.

"If you tax everybody to death, they're all going to leave. And that's what's happening," he added.

Sir Jim's company, Ineos, operates the Forties pipeline which transports about 30% of the UK's North Sea oil.

The government spokesperson said that oil and gas would play an important role in the UK "for decades to come", but they added: "The transition to homegrown clean power is the only way to deliver energy and financial security for families and businesses."

articles.title: An Atlanta teacher spent years warning students away from a locked 26-acre forest outside their school; community organizing has now secured $3 million to begin turning the hidden city land into a public park
articles.summary: US News: An Atlanta teacher spent years warning students to stay away from a locked forest outside their school. Now, after years of community organising, the .
articles.body: An Atlanta teacher spent years warning students to stay away from a locked forest outside their school. Now, after years of community organising, the 26-acre Falling Water Park in southwest Atlanta is set to receive $3 million to help turn the inaccessible greenspace into a public park.Renette Scott, a teacher at Therrell High School, had spent years telling her students not to venture into the woods near the school. The area was closed to the public, and Scott did not know at the time that the city of Atlanta owned the land.The 26-acre forest, known as Falling Water Park, was bought by the city in 2004. It was classified as a “park-in-holding”, which meant the greenspace was protected but remained closed to the public.Scott later joined hands with community members, the nonprofit Park Pride and city officials to push for the development of the land. The effort eventually grew into a community group called Friends of Falling Water Park, which worked for years to bring the forest back into public use. “This is a jewel that we don't know exists,” Scott said.Years of community organisingThe campaign involved meetings, surveys and other activities aimed at building support for the park project. Community members living near the property also became involved in efforts to develop the land.“We had meetings, we did surveys, we had all kinds of activities,” said Deborah Hall, a community organiser involved in the project who lives right outside the park.After years of advocacy, the city of Atlanta was awarded a $2 million state grant to help make the park accessible. The city has said the community's advocacy helped secure the grant.Atlanta will also provide $1 million to match the state funding, taking the total amount available for the project to $3 million.The proposed development includes trails, a boardwalk for fishing and birdwatching, educational signs about wildlife and outdoor recreational areas.Forest and lake could open to visitorsThe planned park would include the wooded property as well as Mount Gilead Lake. Community members involved in the project see the area as a possible destination for birdwatching, fishing and other outdoor activities.Dexter Clemons, a member of Friends of Falling Water Park, said the property could offer several opportunities for visitors.“There are many species that we can put there,” Clemons said. “But to have a fishing area cove over the water where people can come and just relax, of course probably shaded overhead, the trails coming through, there's just so much.”The plans would provide trails through the property and a boardwalk where visitors could fish and watch birds.The project is also expected to change how the land around the park is maintained. Hall said formal development could help remove overgrowth that is not natural to the area while keeping the landscape's natural features.“If it's more formalized, then some of the overgrowth that we see that's not natural to the area will be removed so that we'll have a beautification with what is naturally a part of Georgia,” she said.For Scott, the proposed park is part of a wider effort to address the needs of the surrounding community. She pointed to challenges involving the local economy, greenspace and housing.“This whole area is a desert. We're in a desert economically, a desert with our green space, a desert with our housing. But I think the key to it is how we not only develop it but how we make it sustainable,” Scott said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: North Korea fires two ballistic missiles off east coast in three hours
articles.summary: North Korea launched two missiles off its eastern coast, days after Pyongyang accused the US of driving tensions on the Korean Peninsula through military drills.
articles.body: North Korea launched two missiles off its eastern coast on Sunday, its second set of tests in roughly a week and days after Pyongyang accused the US of driving tensions on the Korean Peninsula through a series of military drills. Just three hours after launching a short-range ballistic missile (SRBM) toward the East Sea on Sunday afternoon, North Korea fired another short-range ballistic missile, according to South Korea’s defense ministry. If the subsequent launch is confirmed to be a ballistic missile, it will mark two consecutive ballistic missile tests by North Korea within a three-hour window. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the first test firing from the Wonsan area around 3 p.m. (2 a.m. ET), identifying the weapon as a ballistic missile. Japan’s defense ministry also said it appeared to be a ballistic missile. Japanese public broadcaster NHK said the projectile had come down outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone. The first projectile flew approximately 450 km (280 miles) and is presumed to belong to the Hwasong-11 series, according to South Korea’s military. The second short-range missile, which was also fired from Wonsan at about 5:50 p.m. (4:50 a.m. ET) flew more than 600 km (373 miles), it said. “South Korean and US intelligence authorities have been tracking and sharing related developments from the initial stage of the launch, and have also shared information regarding the ‘North Korean ballistic missile’ with Japan,” the South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff said. South Korea’s National Security Council condemned the short-range missile launch, which follows a test on September 12. The council urged Pyongyang to immediately cease missile activity, warning the test directly violated UN Security Council resolutions. Japan also lodged a protest through embassy channels in Beijing, according to a Nikkei report. “This series of North Korean actions threatens the peace and security of Japan, the region, and the international community,” Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi was quoted as saying by Nikkei. On Saturday, North Korea dismissed a resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog against Pyongyang’s nuclear program. Pyongyang last week also condemned a US-led naval drill which included South Korea and Japan and which ran from August 29 to September 10 near Guam. North Korea’s Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, on Friday blamed US-led military drills for “ever-worsening” tensions on the Korean Peninsula and vowed no change in the country’s course to strengthen its nuclear arsenal.

articles.title: Puzzling sound in backyard leads homeowner to massive 1,000-year-old treasure
articles.summary: A homeowner digging for a new patio unearthed Denmark's largest known Viking Age silver hoard, containing around 700 objects buried in a clay vessel.
articles.body: A homeowner preparing the yard for a new patio recently made an incredible find — and it's been declared the largest known Viking Age silver hoard ever discovered in Denmark. Officials from North Jutland Museums in northern Denmark announced the discovery on Aug. 31. The hoard was discovered by a private citizen who was preparing the ground for a new tiled terrace, according to a statement from the museum. MYSTERIOUS 3,000-YEAR-OLD HOARD WITH VIOLENTLY SMASHED SWORD EMERGES DURING CONSTRUCTION PROJECT The homeowner, who wished to remain anonymous, called the discovery "the biggest surprise of my life" after stumbling upon the hoard while doing yardwork. "It should have been just a few hours of hard gardening to remove stubborn grass, stones and gravel in relation to a new tiled terrace," the person said. About half an hour into the work, the homeowner struck "something that made a strange sound." The person added, "At first I thought it was old iron or fence wire as well as some potsherds, but when I started digging with my hands, I could suddenly fish one metal object after another out of the ground." ANCIENT VIKING SWORD DISCOVERED 'STICKING UP OUT OF THE GROUND' AFTER 1,300 YEARS The individual said that "after a short time of careful work, it dawned on me that it was jewelry, coins and silver bars." The hoard, which was buried in a clay vessel, is believed to date to the 10th century. It contains around 700 objects and fragments, including silver ingots, bracelets, coins, a small Thor's hammer and various pieces of cut silver. It's Denmark's largest known Viking Age silver hoard, according to North Jutland Museums. The find eclipses the previous record holder — a roughly 14-pound Terslev hoard — and weighs nearly three times as much. DISCOVERY BENEATH SOCCER FIELD REVEALS MASSIVE MEDIEVAL CONVENT LOST FOR CENTURIES Some 320 objects with a total weight of 14 pounds were still in the original clay vessel, while the rest were found in the ground around the site. The homeowner will not keep the treasure. Under Danish law, the hoard belongs to the state — though the finder is eligible to receive a reward. The discovery came after archaeologists recovered six Viking Age gold arm rings from the same area earlier in 2026, Torben Sarauw, head of cultural heritage at North Jutland Museums in northern Denmark, told Fox News Digital. "Almost everything about this discovery surprised me," Sarauw said. "We did not expect that the same area would also produce one of the largest Viking Age silver hoards ever found in Denmark." TREASURE HUNTERS STRIKE GOLD AFTER YEARS OF DISAPPOINTMENT WITH FIND WORTH A FORTUNE He said the hoard "is remarkable because of both its size and its contents. "It contains an unusually large number of silver ingots," Sarauw went on. "One ingot bears runic inscriptions that may have been intended to protect the treasure, while others are marked with Thor's hammers and Christian crosses." Under Danish law, the hoard belongs to the state, though the finder is eligible to receive a reward. He added, "The combination of pagan and Christian symbols, together with the runic inscription and the sheer quantity of silver, makes the find unique." The owner of the hoard must have been "extremely wealthy and of very high social status," Sarauw noted, though the individual's identity is lost to time. "The discovery also indicates that Himmerland was home to a significant center of wealth during the Viking Age, something we are only beginning to understand." Sarauw said hoards were typically buried to safeguard wealth during uncertain times. This treasure may be connected to another silver hoard found nearby several years ago. "One possible explanation is that the owner died before he could recover his treasure, perhaps while traveling or taking part in an overseas expedition. articles.title: California has approved $44 million for 15 land projects; one will protect 14,177 acres, another buys 1,093 desert acres, while an 80-acre property will become a tribal restoration and training site
articles.summary: US News: California’s Wildlife Conservation Board has approved $43.868 million in grants for 15 projects across 11 counties. The projects will support Tribal l.
articles.body: California’s Wildlife Conservation Board has approved $43.868 million in grants for 15 projects across 11 counties. The projects will support Tribal land acquisition, salmon habitat restoration, public access and protection of wildlife corridors.According to California Department of Fish and Wildlife, the funding includes $32 million in climate bond money spread across nine projects. Among the projects is an $11.5 million grant to acquire about 14,177 acres near Callahan in Siskiyou County. Another $7.5 million grant will help buy about 1,093 acres near Yucca Grove in San Bernardino County, while a $700,000 grant will support the purchase of an 80-acre property in Lake County.The projects cover different types of landscapes and conservation work. They include mountain forests, salmon streams, meadows, desert habitat and land connected to Indigenous communities. The Wildlife Conservation Board said the grants support efforts to protect biodiversity and help ecosystems and communities adapt to climate change.14,177 acres to expand forest preserveThe largest land acquisition listed in the announcement will expand the Beaver Valley Headwaters Preserve in Siskiyou County. An $11.5 million grant to The Wildlands Conservancy will fund the purchase of approximately 14,177 acres near Callahan.The purchase will connect more than 20,000 acres of mountain meadows, rivers and forest habitat. The area is important for Scott River salmon and steelhead runs. The project is also intended to help secure streamflow and provide future wildlife-oriented public access.The property provides habitat for coho and Chinook salmon, steelhead, elk, deer, black bear, mountain lion and native bird species.“The Wildlife Conservation Board has been an essential conservation partner in the Scott River region for decades,” said Frazier Haney, executive director of The Wildlands Conservancy.“With its investment today, we can expand the Beaver Valley Headwaters Preserve to over 20,000 acres, facilitating the restoration and rewilding of headwaters that are critically important to coho salmon... We are grateful to WCB for its continued investment in this landscape and the conservation vision we share.”Another project in Siskiyou County focuses directly on streams and fish habitat. A $2.4 million grant to California Trout will support work with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife to restore about eight acres of stream and floodplain habitat near Grenada.The project covers areas along Big Springs Creek and Hole in the Ground Creek, which are tributaries of the Shasta River. Work will include adding gravel, planting native vegetation, building beaver dam analogues and installing log and boulder structures to slow water flow.Meadow restoration and fish habitatThe stream project forms part of a larger 26-mile habitat enhancement effort on the California Department of Fish and Wildlife’s Big Springs Ranch Wildlife Area. The wider effort aims to improve conditions for coho and Chinook salmon, steelhead, Pacific lamprey and migratory waterfowl.“The Big Springs Ranch project represents exactly the kind of on-the-ground impact CalTrout has been working toward in the Shasta River watershed,” said Damon Goodman, Mount Shasta-Klamath regional director for California Trout.The funding also includes $4 million for a meadow restoration project at Johnson Meadow in South Lake Tahoe. The Tahoe Resource Conservation District will carry out the work with the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency.The project will restore 79 acres of mountain meadow along the Upper Truckee River, which is Lake Tahoe’s largest tributary. Planned work includes restoring historical stream channels, repairing riverbanks, removing old utility structures and installing a grade-control structure to reduce erosion near Highway 50.The project will also maintain fish passage for native species, including Lahontan cutthroat trout.“Without the support from the Wildlife Conservation Board, the Johnson Meadow Restoration project would not be possible,” said Andrew Schurr, restoration programme manager for the Tahoe Resource Conservation District.80-acre property to support Tribal restorationOne of the grants focuses on Tribal stewardship and cultural land return. A $700,000 grant to the Tribal EcoRestoration Alliance will fund the purchase of the approximately 80-acre Politsuwi property in Lake County, about five miles north of Lakeport.The property is on the ancestral lands of the Robinson Rancheria, Scotts Valley Band of Pomo Indians and Habematolel Pomo of Upper Lake. It will expand the adjacent EcoCultural Stewardship Training and Demonstration Center.The site is planned as an outdoor learning space for Indigenous-led ecological restoration. The project will protect oak woodlands, wetlands and habitat used by osprey, black-tailed deer and native pollinators.It will also expand job training and cultural programmes for local Tribal communities. “Acquiring the Politsuwi property allows us to grow our hands-on training programmes and deepen Indigenous-led stewardship in Lake County,” said Lindsay Dailey, executive director of the Tribal EcoRestoration Alliance.“This land will give Tribal members and local participants a place to practise cultural restoration, blend traditional knowledge with modern science and care for native habitats for generations to come.”1,093 desert acres to protect tortoise habitatIn the Eastern Mojave, a $7.5 million grant to the Mojave Desert Land Trust will help purchase approximately 1,093 acres near Yucca Grove in San Bernardino County.The private land is surrounded by the Mojave National Preserve. Permanently conserving it will protect habitat for the Mojave desert tortoise, creosote scrub, Joshua tree woodlands and desert washes.The land will be managed to protect sensitive species, preserve natural corridors and prevent development.“This property, located in the greater Mojave National Preserve, represents some of the most ecologically important Mojave desert tortoise habitat remaining in California,” said Kristina Drake, director of conservation ecology for the Mojave Desert Land Trust.“This grant allows us to permanently protect a stronghold for this state-endangered species... Thanks to the Wildlife Conservation Board, we can invest in securing intact habitats that allow all age classes of tortoises to thrive.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Israeli president overrules military to pardon soldier who killed incapacitated Palestinian attacker
articles.summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog pardoned a soldier who shot and killed an incapacitated Palestinian attacker in the occupied West Bank in 2016, despite opposition from the military’s chief of staff.
articles.body: Israeli President Isaac Herzog pardoned a soldier who shot and killed an incapacitated Palestinian attacker in the occupied West Bank in 2016, despite opposition from the military’s chief of staff. Announcing the move on Saturday, Herzog said the decision would allow Elor Azaria, who was in his mandatory military service at the time of the incident, to “continue with his life.” The decision expunges Azaria’s criminal record. The case divided Israeli society as it risked politicizing the military - even playing a role in the resignation of then-Defense Minister Moshe Ya’alon - with many on the right-wing, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, calling for Azaria to receive a pardon. But the Israeli military made clear at the time that it viewed the shooting as a “grave breach of IDF values, conduct and standards of military operations.” Video of the incident showed Azaria, then serving as a combat medic, approaching a Palestinian man, suspected in a knife attack, before shooting him in the head as he lay injured on the street. In a statement on X, Ya’alon blasted the decision to issue the pardon. “The soldier did not claim to have shot the terrorist because he felt his life was in danger, but ‘because he deserved to die,’” Ya’alon said. Addressing Herzog directly, he said, “You decided to erase the criminal record without hearing from the soldier he takes responsibility or regrets his actions.” Herzog, who issued the statement on the eve of Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, said the “circumstances, the length of time passed, and the sorrow Azaria expressed justify enabling him to be allowed to begin a new chapter in his life.” Azaria was sentenced to 18 months in prison for killing Abdel Fattah al-Sharif, who was one of two men accused of stabbing another Israeli soldier in Hebron. Azaria faced up to 20 years in prison after he was convicted; critics said the shorter sentence amounted to a slap on the wrist. He ultimately served only nine months before he was released. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) did not issue a statement after the pardon. But in a July letter in response to the pardon request, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir said “the request should not be granted.” In direct contradiction to Herzog, Zamir’s office stated that Azaria had never expressed sorrow or remorse about the killing. Zamir opposed the pardon because Azaria had not taken responsibility for his actions, and there were no “specific personal circumstances of significant weight” that warranted a pardon. Defense Minister Israel Katz celebrated the pardon, calling it a “humane and appropriate decision.” He said in a statement the “time has come to allow (Azaria) to put the past behind him, rebuild his life and his future.”

articles.title: Palestinian gunman kills Israeli in the West Bank, Israeli soldiers kill motorist
articles.summary: Violence flared in the occupied West Bank on Sunday when a suspected Palestinian gunman shot dead an ​Israeli man, police said, and Israeli soldiers killed a Palestinian ‌motorist who the military said was attempting to run them over.
articles.body: Violence flared in the occupied West Bank on Sunday when a suspected Palestinian gunman shot dead an ​Israeli man, police said, and Israeli soldiers killed a Palestinian ‌motorist who the military said was attempting to run them over. The gunman opened fire from his vehicle at Israelis gathered at a spring near the settlement of ​Neve Tzuf, near Ramallah, according to the Israeli military and ​police. Medics who arrived at the scene of the shooting said ⁠they found a man in a car suffering from critical gunshot ​wounds. He was pronounced dead at hospital, police said. The gunman was located ​a few hours later at a hospital in Ramallah and arrested, police said. Shortly after the shooting, the military said that its forces “eliminated” a Palestinian driver who had ​attempted a ramming attack on soldiers near the settlement of Ganim, ​further north in the West Bank. No soldiers were hurt, it said. Reuters was ‌not ⁠able to immediately verify the soldiers’ account. It was not clear whether the fatal incidents, on the eve of the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur, were connected. Following the incidents, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said ​he had instructed ​security agencies ⁠to beef up their forces and carry out arrests and offensive activities in the area. Palestinian militant group Hamas ​praised the shooting attack but did not claim responsibility ​for it. Violence ⁠has escalated in the West Bank since Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attack on Israel and the ensuing Israeli military offensive in Gaza. The West Bank violence ⁠has ​included a sharp rise in attacks by militant ​settlers on Palestinians, as well as sweeping Israeli military raids and Palestinian attacks on Israelis.

articles.title: TRACE GALLAGHER: Common sense isn't old-fashioned. It's exactly what America needs now
articles.summary: The Common Sense Department segment has become the most memorable 75 seconds on "Fox News @ Night," inspiring a new book and thousands of mugs.
articles.body: Since October 2022, I have anchored a TV show called "Fox News @ Night." Monday to Friday, from 11 p.m. until midnight Eastern time, we cover the news that matters, interview compelling guests and debate the hottest issues. And we do it all in a lively, fast-paced hour of plain-talk television, sending viewers off to bed with a solid grasp of what’s happening in the world and a smile or two as their heads hit the pillow. It’s a modern show, and I don’t just mean the little @ sign in the name. I’m talking about our whole approach to the news. We boil it down and sort it out. We jump right in. And this last one is important: We call BS whenever it’s warranted. Which is often, given all the crap that’s floating around out there. And every night, we include a segment that has become the most memorable 75 seconds in our hour-long show. It’s called the Common Sense Department, and nothing I do on television brings me more joy. TRACE GALLAGHER: COMMON SENSE IS ALIVE IN AMERICA. WE JUST NEED TO LISTEN Every night, I pick something in the news, and I put it through my own filter of hard-earned common sense. You know how TV news works. Every time a major news story breaks—especially a political one—the spin machines start cranking at maximum volume. Suddenly, you’ve got a "panel of experts" flooding your screen, telling you that what you just saw with your own two eyes isn’t actually happening. They’ll look you in the face and insist everything is "deeply nuanced" or "incredibly complex." But let’s be real: Most of the time, it’s not complex at all. My job is simple, even if it’s harder than it looks. I react like a normal, intelligent person who’s been around the block a few times, seen the games people play, and isn’t buying the nonsense anymore. You see it, I see it, and we’re going to call it exactly like it is. That’s why we call it the Common Sense Department. And how do I do it? That’s easy. I rely on the commonsensical lessons I can pluck from my own life and the lives of the people around me. The wisdom I was raised with. What personal experience has taught me along the way. The values of family, faith, sports, community, history and patriotism. Insights drawn from stories exactly like the ones in this book. Just like life, it’s everything mushed together before it’s run through one person’s admittedly quirky brain. Mine. What a rare treat it is! Every night in the Common Sense Department, I really get to be me! And the viewers keep saying, "Give us more." I know this from the ratings. I know it from the social media comments and the emails. I know it from the people I run across when I’m out covering stories and just living my life. And I know it from the mugs. FOX NEWS CHANNEL OUTDRAWS ABC, NBC, CBS IN JULY WEEKDAY PRIMETIME WHILE THUMPING MS NOW, CNN ACROSS BOARD Yes, the mugs. At one point, we printed up some coffee mugs with the snarky slogan, "DID I OFFEND YOU WITH MY COMMON SENSE?" People couldn’t get enough of them. We keep needing to print more. Thousands and thousands and thousands more. The way things are going, our sarcastic call for common sense has really struck a nerve. As I mentioned, our Common Sense Department segments are 75 seconds long. Not two minutes, not one minute—always 75 seconds. And that’s no accident. One time, we tried doing the Common Sense Department in a minute. It felt like a wind sprint. Another time, we said, "Let’s do two minutes." It felt like a drive across Texas with kids in the car. "Are we THERE yet?" CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION "No, we’re NOT there yet—and we’re not stopping at Buc-ees!" That’s one of the great things about common sense. You can pack it into the TV equivalent of a carry-on bag. It isn’t too bulky or hard to handle. And whenever you happen to need it, it’ll be right there. I am not the first person to become a big fan of common sense. Thomas Paine beat me to it by almost 250 years. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Of all the Founding Fathers, Paine is one of the most unlikely and least understood. If you’d known him back in England, you never would have thought he’d amount to much. He washed out as a schoolteacher. His tailor shop failed. He was fired from his job as a tax inspector for "claiming to have inspected goods he did not inspect." He had to sell his house to avoid debtors’ prison. He really, really hated taxes and wrote a pamphlet opposing them. When an American named Benjamin Franklin showed up in London in 1774 as a voice opposing British colonial rule, the two men struck up an instant friendship. It was Franklin who urged Paine to move to Philadelphia, where the American said revolution was in the air. articles.title: ‘People dying, yet crores spent on PM Modi’s birthday’: Tejashwi on Bihar floods
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) leader Tejashwi Yadav on Sunday criticised Bihar’s BJP-led NDA government for spending “crores of rupees” on eve.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) leader Tejashwi Yadav on Sunday criticised Bihar’s BJP-led NDA government for spending “crores of rupees” on events to mark Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday while people in the state were dying in floods.“More than 45 lakh people are affected by floods. Rainfall has been less than 35% this time, causing a part of Bihar to face drought-like conditions. People are dying due to floods, yet hundreds of crores of rupees were squandered on ‘diya-baati’ to mark the prime minister’s birthday,” the Bihar leader of opposition said at a press conference in Patna.Tejashwi Yadav questioned the expenditure on the celebrations and sought details of assistance provided to Bihar through the PM CARES Fund.“Does Bihar come to the Centre’s mind only during elections?” he asked.He also questioned Union agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan’s visit to the state, saying drought-affected areas should have been inspected alongside flood-hit regions.“Did the agriculture minister of the Government of India come and take stock of the drought? He toured the outside areas. Since the agriculture minister had come, he should have visited the drought-affected areas where it rained less than 35% this time, and where farmers’ crops across many hectares have been destroyed,” the RJD leader added.Seeking financial assistance for farmers, Tejashwi Yadav demanded that the “double-engine government” — referring to the BJP being in power at both the Centre and in Bihar — immediately provide at least Rs 15,000 to every farmer affected by drought.He also criticised chief minister Samrat Choudhary, accusing the government of lacking a roadmap and failing to provide relief as tehe stategrapples with floods and drought.The flood situation in Bihar has affected several districts amid rising water levels in the Ganga and other rivers. According to reports citing the state Disaster Management Department, around 40.72 lakh people across 676 gram panchayats in 88 blocks of 16 districts had been affected as of September 20, 2026.The state administration has deployed SDRF and NDRF teams for rescue and relief operations, while community kitchens, relief camps and boats are being used to assist affected residents.Political parties and leaders have also contributed to relief efforts. The Hindustani Awam Morcha (Secular) donated Rs 11 lakh to the Bihar Chief Minister’s Relief Fund, while its MPs, MLAs and MLCs contributed one month’s salary each. The BJP donated Rs 51 lakh, while its national president Nitin Nabin pledged three months’ salary. Chief minister Samrat Choudhary also donated one month’s salary to the relief fund.(With ANI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Can't stop BJP alone': Owaisi opens alliance door to 'like-minded' parties in UP
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: With Uttar Pradesh set for assembly polls in 2027, AIMIM supremo Asaduddin Owaisi has thrown open the possibility of an alliance with parti.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: With Uttar Pradesh set for assembly polls in 2027, AIMIM supremo Asaduddin Owaisi has thrown open the possibility of an alliance with parties looking to prevent the BJP from returning to power for a third straight term, saying no opposition party can take on the BJP alone.Owaisi, speaking to news agency ANI on Sunday, invited “like-minded” parties for talks and said AIMIM was prepared to work with them if the common objective was to keep the BJP out of power.“We do not want the BJP government to be formed for a third time in Uttar Pradesh. If anyone does not want the BJP to form the government, they can talk to us. We are ready to work with you to stop the BJP from coming to power. But it is important to understand that you cannot stop the BJP alone,” he said.His outreach comes as political parties begin preparing for the 2027 contest in Uttar Pradesh, where the BJP has been in power since 2017 under the leadership of Yogi Adityanath.Owaisi, however, cautioned against viewing the coming election through the lens of previous polls, saying the political contest would have its own set of challenges.“Assembly elections are coming. It won’t be the 2014 election, nor the 2017 election, nor the 2019 election, nor the 2022 election. This is going to be a completely different election,” he said.‘We asked for six seats’ in BiharOwaisi pointed to AIMIM’s experience in Bihar to underline the party’s position on alliances. He said the party had approached several opposition leaders before the Bihar elections, seeking an alliance and asking for six seats, but the proposal did not find support.“We said this in Bihar as well, and our president, Akhtarul Iman, wrote a letter not just to the RJD or the Congress, but to all the CPI and Communist Party leaders. We said, ‘Please give us six seats.’ But they did not agree,” he said.Despite the lack of an alliance, Owaisi said AIMIM would continue building its organisation in Uttar Pradesh. He claimed the party’s leadership had developed from the grassroots and said its workers were already active across constituencies.“Our party organisation has become quite strong. Our leadership has emerged at the grassroots level, and our leaders have a strong connection with the ground. The party is working hard on its part,” he said.Hyderabad MP said alliance talks would not determine AIMIM’s organisational plans.“Whether we are in talks with whom or not is a different matter, but we will continue our work. If you want to stop the BJP, come and talk to us. We are ready to work with you,” he said.Owaisi targets BJP, SP over ‘hooliganism’Turning to the Yogi-led BJP government, Owaisi alleged that several promises made by the party remained unfulfilled. He raised issues including governance, law and order, electricity and land disputes, saying these would become important themes in the election.He also criticised the previous Samajwadi Party government, drawing a comparison between the two regimes.“When the Samajwadi Party was in power, one kind of hooliganism used to happen. Someone else did it. Now, under their government, a different kind of hooliganism is happening,” Owaisi said.He also sought the public release of the SIT report into the alleged Ram Mandir embezzlement case and questioned how accused persons were securing bail.“Why isn’t the SIT report released to the public? Why doesn’t the government release it? And why are those people getting bail? How are they getting bail? It’s strange. This will also be a big talking point,” he said.AIMIM steps up UP groundworkAIMIM has already begun preparing for the 2027 election, with Owaisi saying the party is touring constituencies to strengthen its organisation and gauge local concerns.He said he was in Kanpur on Sunday and would visit Shravasti in six days, followed by Azamgarh. Public meetings are also planned in three or four constituencies in western Uttar Pradesh.“The sole purpose is to strengthen our party organisation for the upcoming elections,” Owaisi said.He added that staying connected with voters was central to the party’s preparations.“By staying among the people, we can understand their suffering on the ground and highlight the difficulties this government has created for them,” he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Italy to ban veils in schools, limit foreign students per class, Meloni says
articles.summary: Italy is preparing to ban face coverings in schools and to cap the number of foreign students per class, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Sunday as she played up her right-wing credentials at a youth event organised by her party.
articles.body: Italy is preparing to ban face coverings in schools and to cap the number of foreign students per class, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Sunday as she played up her right-wing credentials at a youth event organised by her party. Italy is among the European countries most exposed to migrant arrivals because of its central Mediterranean location, making migration a hot-button issue and a major challenge for successive governments. The integration of migrants, particularly those from Muslim-majority countries, remains contentious in Italian politics and society. Debates over religious symbols, cultural integration, citizenship rules and immigration policy frequently polarize public opinion. “A measure will soon be presented to a Cabinet meeting to legally establish a maximum number of foreign students per class. It also requires parents of foreign students facing serious difficulties integrating into the school system to learn Italian and bans burqas and niqabs in schools,” Meloni told an annual gathering of the youth wing of her Brothers of Italy party. “If there is only one child in a class who doesn’t understand Italian, that child will likely be able to learn the language and integrate quickly with the help of classmates and teachers. articles.title: Healthcare goes digital: When doctors go behind the app wall, who gets left behind?
articles.summary: India News: What if your phone becomes the first thing you need to see a doctor?As healthcare increasingly moves from hospital counters and paper records to apps .
articles.body: What if your phone becomes the first thing you need to see a doctor?As healthcare increasingly moves from hospital counters and paper records to apps and online portals, access to care is becoming closely tied to access to technology.For many patients, digital healthcare can mean quicker consultations, easier access to medical records and fewer trips to hospitals. But for others, particularly older people, rural communities, low-income families and those with limited digital literacy, the shift can add another layer of difficulty.The problem is not simply whether a person owns a smartphone. Patients may struggle with internet connectivity, downloading and navigating apps, remembering passwords and OTPs, uploading documents or understanding information presented online.In many households, a single smartphone is shared by several family members, while caregivers often become the bridge between patients and digital health services.As government and private healthcare services increasingly encourage, and in some cases require, people to use digital platforms, a larger question is emerging: Is technology making healthcare more accessible, or creating a new barrier to accessing it?When the smartphone becomes the gateway to healthcareDigital health has opened up several ways for patients to manage their care remotely. People can consult doctors online, monitor blood sugar through connected devices, receive medication and appointment reminders, and access diet and educational resources without making frequent hospital visits.Telemedicine became particularly important during the Covid-19 pandemic, when lockdowns made physical consultations difficult. But the experience also exposed how uneven access to digital healthcare could be.A DIG-EQUITY study published in The Times of India, examining the experiences of people with diabetes, caregivers, healthcare providers, policymakers and community organisations in urban and rural Tamil Nadu, found significant differences in how people used digital health services.Younger patients were generally more comfortable with smartphones, health applications and teleconsultations, while many older people needed family members to book appointments, join consultations or access medical reports.For some, physical limitations added to the problem. Impaired vision or hearing, as well as difficulty handling smartphones, could make navigating digital platforms harder.Even among younger people, digital access did not automatically translate into a preference for online care. Some people with type 1 diabetes continued to prefer in-person consultations because of the need for physical examinations.The digital divide is also closely linked to where people live and what they can afford.Urban patients are more likely to have reliable internet connections, smartphones and access to digital services. A study published in Nature, examining barriers to digital health transformation in India, found that the challenges went beyond simply having a smartphone or internet connection.The study identified poor network coverage and inadequate IT infrastructure, the high cost of devices and digital systems, a lack of technical expertise, language and communication barriers, and difficulties faced by users among the major challenges.For patients, these barriers can have very practical consequences. The study noted that some had to rely on family members' smartphones to attend teleconsultations, while the cost of smart devices could limit access to mobile health applications.The findings suggest that digital access cannot be measured simply by whether someone owns a phone. Reliable connectivity, affordability, digital skills, language accessibility and the availability of human support all influence whether a patient can actually use digital healthcare.That distinction becomes particularly important as healthcare services increasingly move online. Putting a service on a digital platform does not automatically make it accessible to everyone.ABHA and the push towards connected healthcareIndia's digital health infrastructure is expanding rapidly. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), through platforms such as ABHA, is aimed at creating a connected digital health ecosystem, while eSanjeevani has widened access to telemedicine.With hundreds of millions of ABHA IDs created and telemedicine consultations running into hundreds of millions, the scale of this shift is significant.But the benefits of digital healthcare are not evenly experienced.The gap becomes particularly visible when digital systems are introduced at the hospital level. For some patients, the shift has not removed queues; it has created an additional one.Rekha (name changed), a patient at the Delhi National Cancer Institute, said patients earlier had to wait in a single OPD queue, with doctors arriving around 8am. According to her, the process now involves generating a token through the ABHA app before reaching the hospital, followed by another number at the reception.“Earlier there used to be only one OPD line and the doctors used to arrive at 8am. Now they have made it mandatory to download the ABHA app and apply for a token number. Then we get another number from reception, and doctors arrive at 10am. Several patients need immediate care, but this extra queue has made life a bit more difficult,” she said.For those without a smartphone or reliable internet connection, Rekha said the process can begin hours before they reach the doctor. Some patients, she said, arrive around midnight or 1am and spend the night waiting because they cannot access the network or generate a digital token.Those with smartphones may apply through the ABHA app around 5am and reach the hospital by 7am, she said, only to wait again at reception before seeing a doctor later in the morning.Dr Manisha Arora, Director, Internal Medicine, CK Birla Hospital, Delhi, said ABHA should remain a facilitator rather than become a gateway to treatment.“A patient should never feel that access to technology determines access to healthcare,” she said, noting that patients without an ABHA ID, smartphone or internet connectivity should continue to be able to register physically and receive the same clinical care.She stressed that hospitals should adopt a digital-first, not digital-only, approach.“That means retaining manual registration counters, providing assisted kiosks and having dedicated digital-support personnel, particularly for elderly and first-time users.”Insurance goes digital, but payment and paperwork remain a burdenDigital insurance processes are another area where patients can struggle. Families dealing with hospitalisation may simultaneously have to navigate e-KYC, pre-authorisation, co-payments, deductions and non-payable items.Manivannan Selvaraj, Founder and Managing Director, Kauvery Group of Hospitals, said translating a clinical treatment plan into a pre-authorisation submission, and then managing the queries and follow-ups that come back, involves a long chain of steps that a patient is neither equipped nor educated to handle, and should not have to handle while they or a family member is unwell.“Sometimes delays or claim issues arise because documentation is incomplete rather than because of a medical concern,” Arora said, stressing that hospital insurance desks need to act as patient counsellors, explaining the process rather than merely uploading documents.“True digital accessibility is when technology works in the background and the patient still experiences a human interface at the front,” she said.At 65, Amarnath (name changed) has an insurance policy but says managing it digitally has become difficult. He is often unsure about when he can claim, when premiums are due and how to complete the process online, leaving his son to handle the details for him.“I have an insurance policy, but I often don’t know when I can make a claim, when the premium is due or how to complete these processes online. My son manages it for me. At my age, it is not always easy to visit a centre every time I need to check my policy or make a claim. If healthcare is becoming digital, these services should also be made accessible to elderly people, so that we can manage them ourselves without having to depend on others,” he said.He also highlighted how the growing use of digital payments in hospitals can create another challenge for elderly patients unfamiliar with the technology. Having a UPI-enabled phone does not necessarily mean being comfortable using it, particularly during a medical emergency when payments may need to be made quickly.“I have UPI on my phone, but for people of our generation, it is difficult to become fully comfortable with the process and make an immediate payment, especially during a health emergency. This is something that should also be addressed,” he said.Covid era showed that systems still struggleThe pandemic offered an early and stark example of how closely technology and healthcare had become intertwined.While telemedicine and digital systems helped patients access services during lockdowns, other parts of the healthcare chain showed that digitisation alone could not solve problems of capacity and access.As reported by The Times of India earlier, delays in Covid testing became a major concern during the second wave. Udham Singh, 22, developed high fever, severe cough, body ache and breathlessness after his sample was collected for an RT-PCR test. His report, which confirmed Covid infection, came several days after the sample was taken.“I would have landed in an ICU had I waited for some more time. The element of uncertainty due to delay also caused extreme mental trauma,” Singh said.For patients waiting at home, the delay was not merely an inconvenience. It affected decisions about treatment and isolation. Some families also faced difficulties maintaining quarantine while waiting for test results.Priya Jaiswal, a resident of Old Delhi, recalled how a network outage during the pandemic left her dependent on officials for essential medicines. With her internet connection down, she could not use UPI to make payments or order medicines online, leaving her waiting for officials to arrive at her home.“We had to wait for hours for officials to arrive and hand over the medicines while we were in quarantine. Even online consultations became difficult because of continuous power cuts at a time when we needed healthcare the most,” she said.The surge in demand for Covid testing also put pressure on government laboratories to issue digital reports on time, highlighting another challenge for digital healthcare: a digital interface is only as effective as the system supporting it.Covid-19 vaccination certificates also affected people's travel and employment plans.Varghese Thomas, a youth from the city, told TOI that five people in his group had taken their first vaccine dose around the same time, but only one had received the certificate nearly 40 days later.“When we applied for jobs, prospective employers were asking us about the vaccination. They wanted us to produce the certificate,” he said.Registering through Co-WIN was another difficulty for people in rural areas.As reported by The Times of India earlier, 68-year-old Adhi Kesavan from Gudiyattam in Tamil Nadu's Vellore district had to travel around 5-7 km with his wife to a common service centre to register for vaccination.Kesavan did not own a smartphone or know how to use one. He was directed to the centre by his panchayat head, who told him that his details could be registered there and that the hospital would contact him when a vaccine became available.“I heard from our panchayat head that we can get vaccinated if we register at the e-sevai maiyyam. Our number will be given to the hospitals nearby and we will get a call once the vaccine is ready,” Kesavan said. He was still waiting for that call.Digital healthcare cannot mean digital-only healthcareIndia's digital-health expansion will ultimately be measured not only by how many people are connected to the system, but also by whether those who are not can still access care with the same ease and dignity.The goal should not be to make healthcare digital at any cost. It should be to make healthcare more accessible, using technology when it helps, and providing human support when it doesn't.Because for a patient struggling to connect, navigate an app, remember an OTP or make a digital payment, the smartphone should never become another obstacle between them and a doctor.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Museum and library in Leek set to reopen after revamp
articles.summary: The venues, which have been refreshed as part of a £4m restoration, reopen on Monday.
articles.body:
A library and museum is set to reopen after a revamp created a "vibrant, modern and flexible space", said project leaders.

The amenities in the Grade II-listed Nicholson Institute in Leek, Staffordshire, were modernised as part of a £4m restoration which has also brought the building's lower ground floor back into use.

Hayley Coles, Staffordshire County deputy leader, added the library included a quality book stock, comfortable study space and "inspiring children's library".

The building's art gallery, which is set to open next month, has also been updated and a mural by Robert Timmis restored.

Staffordshire Moorlands District Council said it led the project using government funding as part of the wider generation of Leek town centre.

"These spaces have been re-imagined to improve the experience for visitors and library users and they've been given a fresh, contemporary look which respects the heritage of the building," said Matt Swindlehurst, cabinet member for leisure and tourism.

"We were pleased to have funded the improvements which have helped create a welcoming, vibrant, modern and flexible space that also complements the proud and rich heritage of the Nicholson building," said Coles, who is also the county's cabinet member for communities and culture.

"The library is now ideally placed and fully equipped to meet local residents' needs."

The district council will run the museum and gallery and their events programmes with volunteers from the Friends of the Nicholson Institute.

The authority worked with the county council who the district council said hold the Nicholson Institute in trust and contributed to the cost of the library refurbishment.

articles.title: Richard Hammond thanks 999 crews on Elvington crash anniversary
articles.summary: Richard Hammond was seriously injured in a jet dragster crash at Elvington in September 2006.
articles.body:
Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has thanked emergency services for their help on the 20th anniversary of the crash in which he was nearly killed.

Hammond was seriously injured in September 2006 when the 320mph (515km/h) jet-powered Vampire dragster he was driving veered off the track at Elvington airfield, near York, during filming for the BBC show.

In an Instagram post, Hammond said he wanted to thank the members of the staff who rescued him and supported him following the accident "from the bottom of my heart".

In the post, he spoke of the events of that day and said he would be "forever grateful" to all those who helped him in the aftermath of the crash.

He wrote: "Twenty years ago today, I came to an abrupt stop upside down in a Yorkshire field, convinced I was about to die."

He said he recalled having pulled the lever to release the car's parachute before trying to steer it away from disaster, "but disaster was, it seemed, my fate".

"Having done everything I could to avert it, I gave myself over to that fate," he said.

A front tyre had blown on the car and Hammond said in his post that he did not scream during the ensuing crash.

He explained that while "it wasn't frightening", it had "simply occurred to me that the next thing on my to do list was to die".

The Top Gear star spent two weeks in a coma after the crash and returned to the show in early 2007.

In 2023, he spoke of how he believed his memory may have been affected by the accident.

In his post on social media marking the anniversary of the crash, Hammond said: "I am only here today to note this anniversary and write these words because of the work of the many people involved in rescuing me from the shattered car, flying me to hospital and treating me there."

Hammond went on to name members of the Yorkshire Air Ambulance and aftercare teams who helped him, saying he would be "forever grateful" to them.

He said he would not have had the lucky career breaks, amazing adventures around the world and two of the "happiest, kindest, most wonderfully talented and loving daughters" if he had not been helped that day.

"Thank you all from the bottom of my heart," he added.

Hammond was also injured in a serious crash during a practice run for an electric car race 11 years later in Switzerland in June 2017, when his vehicle left the road, tumbled down a hillside and burst into flames close to a house.

After leaving Top Gear with co-hosts Jeremy Clarkson and James May in 2015, the trio reunited for The Grand Tour, which they presented until 2024.

articles.title: Beloved Mexican food disappearing from restaurant menus across America
articles.summary: Tamale entrees have dropped 7.8% on Mexican restaurant menus across the United States, and the grueling labor behind each masa batch is a key reason.
articles.body: The tamale was once a familiar presence on Mexican restaurant menus in the United States, sharing space with tacos, burritos and enchiladas. Increasingly, though, diners looking for one may have to search. Tamale entrées have dropped 7.8% from menus over the past five years, according to Technomic's Ignite Menu data comparing the second quarters of 2021 and 2026. One reason may be a basic restaurant calculation: Tamales require considerable labor for something diners expect to be relatively inexpensive. POPULAR TEX-MEX CHAIN ABRUPTLY SHUTTERS REMAINING RESTAURANTS ACROSS AMERICA AMID INDUSTRY STRUGGLES Robert Mahon, director of operations for Mahon Hospitality Group, runs Amor Loco and Toro Loco in New York City, neither of which serves tamales. Mahon enjoys tamales himself and said his restaurants have discussed offering them, but the economics can be difficult. "Even though the ingredients might not be so costly, it's more the labor," Mahon told Fox News Digital. "It's so labor-intensive." That labor becomes apparent at Taquería Picoso in Alexandria, Virginia, where executive chef Elio Gomez keeps tamales on the menu. Gomez said his process takes about three days. His restaurant sources corn from Mexico, then cooks it through an overnight nixtamalization process. The corn is ground into masa, while fillings and banana leaves are prepared separately. The masa must then be mixed with fat, broth and salt and aerated to achieve the right consistency before the tamales can be assembled, carefully wrapped and cooked. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Training someone to do all that takes time, too. Gomez said he spent months working alongside the employee who now makes his tamales. Even with a recipe, Gomez said, a cook must learn how the masa should feel and how to wrap each tamale properly, so it doesn't dry out during cooking. All that work goes into an item that still doesn't generate taco-level demand. "No, definitely it's not the same demand as a taco, for example," Gomez said. Mahon said his customers aren't clamoring for tamales either. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "They're not walking out of our restaurants if they don't have a tamale," Mahon said. "It's not expected as a staple anymore." Price presents another complication. Gomez charges $6 for a tamale, a price he considers inexpensive given the work involved. But some customers remember much cheaper versions. Yet the tamale's declining presence on restaurant menus doesn't necessarily mean the food itself is disappearing. Gomez, who grew up in Mexico City, remembers tamales as an everyday breakfast food sold by street vendors in the morning. In the United States, he sees them being treated more as a special food associated with holidays and family gatherings. articles.title: Trump says monumental arch in Washington, DC will also be military complex
articles.summary: Plans for the arch had been met with opposition along with other projects by the US president to reshape capital city.
articles.body:
A planned “triumphal arch” near some of the most iconic landmarks in Washington, DC, will also be a military complex used to store drones and other military equipment, according to United States President Donald Trump.

The changes were made at the request of the military and for “National Security purposes,” Trump posted on his social media platform on Sunday.

The project would now be used to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage,” Trump said. “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World.”

Trump first proposed building a monumental arch last year to mark 250 years of US independence, saying it would be akin to other famed arches like the Arc de Triomphe built in Paris after World War Two, but “the biggest one of all”.

On Sunday, the US president did not provide details on the new design, which was previously planned to be a lofty 76-metre-high (250-foot) arch that would tower above many other landmarks in the capital. By law, the height of new construction in the city is generally restricted.

Trump’s arch project has faced criticism ever since then for its size and location, and for potentially obscuring views of the Arlington National Cemetery, the country’s famed resting place for war veterans.

In February, three veterans of the Vietnam War filed a lawsuit against the plan, saying it would block the view between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial, erected to honour the US president who oversaw the Civil War. The view from the monument, the veterans said in a court filing, was “carefully designed to symbolise the unification of the country after the Civil War and the strength of a united nation”. Any major monument around the capital, the lawsuit also argued, would need approval from the US Congress. A judge ordered the Trump administration to provide notice of any work on the monument, but courts have not ruled on the larger challenge yet.

The Trump-appointed US Commission of Fine Arts, a key agency involved in the project, approved a design in April that featured statues of golden lions at the base of the arch, and golden eagles and a winged angel atop a baroque arch resembling the one in Paris.

The Federal Aviation Administration said last week the arch would not be a hazard to the nearby Reagan Washington National Airport, but would need a warning beacon on top.

The monumental arch is one of several Trump projects in the capital to receive public pushback.

On Saturday, thousands rallied, and some protesters formed a human chain around the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, the landmark along the Potomac River waterfront built to honour the 35th US President John F Kennedy. Trump has threatened to demolish the venue if he is not allowed to add his name to it, saying that is the only way to ensure it gets enough funding to survive.

Trump is also overseeing a $400m controversial project at the White House, where the East Wing of the complex was demolished to make way for an 8,400sq m (90,000sq ft) ballroom with an impenetrable underground bunker. Historic preservation groups filed a lawsuit to stop that project, but last month the US Supreme Court allowed construction to continue .

Like the triumphal arch, Trump has also justified the need for the new ballroom on national security grounds and has referred to it as a “military complex”.

articles.title: Rutgers' Greg Schiano crashes out on official after costly penalty in tough loss to USC
articles.summary: Greg Schiano knocked down a field marker in a fiery sideline tantrum after a controversial illegal substitution call during Rutgers' 42-35 loss to USC.
articles.body: Rutgers was very, very close to pulling off an all-time upset against No. 12 USC on Saturday. If it wasn’t for an ill-timed Pick Six in the third quarter and a questionable illegal substitution penalty, the Trojans may have been under the microscope a bit more Sunday morning. In the midst of the Scarlet Knights’ defeat, head coach Greg Schiano had one of the wilder crash outs of the year. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! USC had the ball and was trying to drive down the field to get another score that likely would have sent more of the fans in Piscataway, New Jersey, home early. The referees called a play dead over an inadvertent whistle that set up another third-down play. It would have been 3rd-and-7 from USC’s own 28-yard line. But Rutgers was called for an illegal substitution that moved the ball up a few more yards. Needless to say, Schiano was irate. He was seen on the CBS broadcast giving one of the side judges an earful. One of his assistants tried desperately to keep Schiano off the field as he got animated. Schiano ended up knocking down the field marker in his tantrum. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE USC quarterback Jayden Maiava threw an incomplete pass to force a fourth down. But he completed a 32-yard pass on his next attempt to keep the drive alive. USC would turn the ball over on downs but Rutgers couldn’t get anything together on their next possession. The Trojans and Scarlet Knights traded touchdowns on their next two drives respectively. USC would hang on for the 42-35 win. It was one of the best games Rutgers played all season after being trounced by UMass to start the year and then suffering a defeat against Boston College. The Scarlet Knights had 460 total yards in the loss. Quarterback Dylan Lonergan had three touchdowns and two interceptions. USC’s King Miller rushed for 102 yards and a score.
